speechtext: Hon. J. A. CALDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 146, to amend the Chinese Immigration Act.

Explain
this.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The most important
amendment contained in the Bill will be found in the first section. As the law now stands, Chinese merchants coming to Canada are admitted without paying a head tax, on the production of a certificate of identity which is issued by the officers of the Chinese Government and vised by the British Consular Officers in China. It has been found during the past year-I think to some extent owing to conditions in China-that a good deal of abuse has prevailed in connection with the issuing of these certificates. Consequently we propose to abolish the certificates and require every Chinese merchant landing on our western coasts to satisfy the controller of immigration there as to the' bona fides of his status.

Is this controller of
Chinese immigration an official of this Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes. The second amendment is to the effect that a board of inquiry, appointed under the general Immigration Act, may determine the question as to whether or not a person of Chinese race has legally entered Canada. Under the law as it now stands, if any question arises in that connection it must be tried by a magistrate. Under our general immigration law, applying to all other people, these cases are heard by a board of inquiry and determined by them, so it is proposed to make the two laws uniform in that respect. The third amendment relates to section 18 of the Chinese Immigration Act. That section deals with and enumerates the prohibited classes-for example paupers, lunatics and others of that category, The provision in the present Chinese Act does not go as far as a similar provision in our general law, and the object of this amendment is to make the two laws the same in that respect-that is to define in both our Acts, the general Act and the Chinese Immigration Act, the classes that are prohibited and to make them the same. Then there is a further provision to this effect: Under the law as it now stands, Chinese, other than the non-immigrant class, who enter Canada are required to pay a head tax of $500. They, however, have the right to return to China. That is called "registering out." They obtain a certificate when they leave and under that certificate they are entitled to return to Canada at any time within the year without again paying the head tax. It is proposed to make the period a two-year period instead of, as at present, one year. Then there is a fifth amendment to this effect: That where a person of the Chinese race has entered Canada illegally-if he belongs to, say, any of the prohibited classes, and has succeeded in securing entry to Canada illegally, and is afterwards found-the question as to his right to remain in Canada shall be determined by the controller of Chinese immigration. There is, of course, in all cases an appeal to the minister, as undtsr the general Immigration Act. In addition there are a number of minor amendments which deal largely with small matters of administration.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. C. BALLANTYNE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the very able Budget presented to the House by my colleague the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) will receive very general approval throughout the country, and I have been very much gratified to hear the warm words of commendation that have fallen from hon. members on both sides of the House who have so far taken part in this debate.
I do not intend to refer in any great detail to the Budget, but one or two salient features of it will, I am sure, appeal to hon. members and to the people generally. The revenues for last year exceeded the ordinary expenses, including all pensions and current war charges by $69,400,000, and exceeded the sum total of the ordinary expenses, together with the regular charges to capital and war, by $12,298,000. I am sure hon. members will agree with me that, considering the very trying year the country has passed through, special thanks are due to our able minister for the skilful manner in which he has looked after the national finances, particularly in view of the very significant fact that he has been able to do so without any fresh borrowings. Another very gratifying feature is that our revenue for the year 1920-21 exceeded that of the previous fiscal year by the large sum of $83,000,000.
I recognize, Sir, that great freedom of debate is allowed to hon. members when speaking on the Budget, but I must say that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) last night exceeded, in my humble opinion at any rate, the usual bounds of courtesy and failed to maintain that high standard of debate which is associated with our deliberations when he took up the time of this House by reading imaginary letters evolved from his peculiarly fertile brain. If the hon. member in taking this course had refrained from connecting the names of ministers of the Crown holding two of the most important portfolios in the Government, no one in this House would have taken any exception to the playful diversion that appears to appeal to the hon. member in writing imaginary letters. But I want to say that your Honour very properly described the action of the hon. member last night when you reminded him that it was in very bad taste.
I am sorry that the hon. member is not in his seat at the present time. I am satisfied that he had an ulterior motive when he wrote those imaginary letters. I do not consider that it was either good taste or good political tactics for the hon. member to weave together the letter of the hon. Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue (Mr. Wigmore), the reply of the right hon. Prime Minister, (Mr. Meighen) and his imaginary letter that was supposed to have been written by me as Minister of Marine and Fisheries to my colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. McCurdy). I can imagine that when the

general election is on certain politicians of a peculiar type will take care on the hustings all over the country to say:	If you
will turn to the pages of Hansard you will find first of all the letter of the Minister of Customs, then the reply of the right hon. Prime Minister, and also a letter written by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the Minister of Public Works. And what will follow? The usual declaration, that these men occupying the treasury benches are making an unfair use of their power in trying to influence business to the companies that they may happen to be connected with.
I find it difficult, Sir, to keep within the bounds of parliamentary language in referring to an incident that has never before occurred in this House, and I am sure will never be repeated. Aside from the hon. member for Brome, I do not think there is a single gentleman in this House who would have invented such an imaginary letter and placed it on the pages of Hansard. It is true that I am a director of various companies, and I have on a previous occasion stated to this House that I have no apology to make for holding those positions, for necessarily a business man must be a member of several boards of directors. But I want to point out to my hon. friend from Brome that two of the companies that he credits me in this imaginary letter with being a director of are companies in which I have no such control. Therefore his imagination led him astray in this instance. Sir, I have already taken up too much of the valuable time of this House in referring to the tactics of my hon. friend from Brome. Such tactics are beneath the contempt of every hon. member, and therefore I shall refrain from making any further allusion to them.
In connection with this incident, however, Mr. Speaker, I think it is the duty of this House to so amend the rules that in the future we may have no recurrence of this practice of producing imaginary letters. As I have already stated, I do not know of any other hon. member who would be so lacking in good taste as to follow in the steps of the hon. member for Brome, but at the same time the rules of the House should not allow such imaginary letters to be officially recorded on the pages of Hansard with the names of ministers of the Crown attached thereto.
Now, Sir, I desire to pass from that to the remarks of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). No

man holds the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's in higher esteem than I do; he is a man very highly thought of in this blouse and throughout the country. There was a time when he and I could see eye to eye on the matter of the tariff, but in these days our views are, of course, totally divergent/

maintopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Quebec East .says, "Hear, hear." But I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that my views have not changed; those of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's have. I was somewhat amused to hear the veteran statesman, speaking officially for hon. gentlemen opposite, voice his disappointment that the Government had not seen fit to revise the tariff, and express the view that a general revision should have taken place at this session. I was reminded of the speeches of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). I recall, as all hon. gentlemen do, his statements in this House and outside of the House that the Government hold no mandate from the people; that we have no right to change the tariff. Yet in his speech yesterday the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's expressed deep regret at the decision of the Government not to make any general revision of the tariff.
I was surprised also at the remarks made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's with regard to free trade. As was evident to every hon. member -on this side, he skilfully baited his hook with the very best bait he could get and dangled it for some time in front of our friends of the Agrarian group. He said: "I am a free trader as far as theory goes." He appealed to them and said: "You think you are free traders, but you are not. What is the use of thinking any longer that you are a free trade group? After all, there is a great similarity between the Agrarian party in this House and the party to which I belong." But Sir, I find it difficult to reconcile the arguments of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's with the speeches that have been delivered in this House and outside by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), leader of the Agrarian party and by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). Every one will agree that the hon. member for Red Deer is an out-and-out free trader. He has never hidden his light under a bushel; in this House and everywhere he speaks he

says that he.is a pronounced free trader of the Cobden type. The leader of the Agrarian party, the hon. member for Marquette, is equally a pronounced free trader, except that he is of a somewhat more prudent turn of mind; instead of cutting off the heads of the protectionist voters in this country at one fell swoop he is in favour of a slow, lingering death. But so far as the abolition of protection is concerned his views are identical with those of the hon. member for Red Deer. I need not dwell further on that subject; we accept the free trade sentiments so eloquently expressed by the hon. member for Red Deer and by the hon. member for Marquette, and we realize that if they ever reach power they will wipe out every vestige of protection and carry out the policies that they have enunciated. But, Sir, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's made another statement yesterday which differs a little from the views which he has enunciated in the past. Referring to the establishment of new industries and the investment of new capital in this country, he said:
If there are any people In Canada who are contemplating the establishment of new lines of business in which they feel that tariff protection is necessary, I do them a friendly service when I say: "Don't do it," because anybody who counts upon the continuance of a protective policy is bound to find that he is pursuing a delusion. If any outside capitalist purposes coming to Canada to start some industry which he believes can only be kept alive by protection, again, I advise him not to come. I say, Sir, that the policy of indiscriminate fostering of industries in that way, without regard to economic conditions, is not a sound one.
Those are the words of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, speaking in this House yesterday. But let us look at the words to which he gave utterance when speaking on the Budget on May 18, 1920. His remarks will be found on page 2505 of Hansard of that year. Here is what he had to say then about infant industries:
Now, I would be always willing to help an infant industry if I were sure that when the infant grew up it would accept the full responsibility of manhood.
Further on he says:
I repeat, I would willingly help an infant industry, and as between protection and bounties, I think I would prefer the bounties.
I think all will agree that the views of the hon. member as expressed last year on the Budget, so far as new industries are concerned, are diametrically opposed to those which he now expresses. I have very
often heard hon. gentlemen who compose the Agrarian group say that they are against the policy of protection but that a still more vicious system is that of bounties; yet the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's stated last year in this House that he was in favour of bounties. Then he went on to point out-and I do not disagree with him-the beneficial results which accrued through the granting of bounties to the iron and steel industry by the government of which he was a member.
The policy of the party to which I have the honour to belong is well-known; under our young, able, progressive, and distinguished leader we stand four-square in this House and from the Atlantic to the Pacific on the policy of moderate protection. We believe in a policy that will not only keep all the industries going which we now have, but will induce new capital to come to this country. We favour the establishment of all the new industries that it is possible for us to induce to come here. They will be treated fairly. We will not give them a tariff "as high as Haman's gallows," nor do we stand for or believe in free trade. But we do believe in the policy of moderate protection, and so long as we occupy the seats of office we will do our very best to encourage new industries to come in. And I know of no country which offers the same golden opportunities to capital and to business men as this country in which we have the good fortune to live. Especially is that true with regard to my own province. We have a quiet, law-abiding people; we have a splendid labour market; we have good water-powers. While all the provinces of Canada offer excellent opportunities for the establishment of new industries, there is none better than the good old province of Quebec that I have the honour to represent in this House.
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's expressed regret that the Government had . accepted from Great Britain the free gift of one modern oil-burning light cruiser, two destroyers and two submarines. He went on to state that, in these days of peace and in view of the sentiment of the country in favour of economy-which he thought was not being exercised by the Government, but which is-we were not warranted in accepting these ships from the Mother Country. He stated that they were a white elephant on the hands of the Government and the people of Canada. I stated very plainly in this House last year, and I reiterate

the statement now, that we are not increasing, nor have we increased, the naval expenditure of this country by one copper. We are carrying out, as regards naval affairs, the policy that was placed upon the statute books of Canada by the passing of the Naval Service Act in the year 1910. What did we do? We said that it would not be right to continue to spend a sum of money equal to what we are spending now (two and a half million dollars) on old, obsolete ships-the old Niobe, thirty years of age, tied up to the dock at Halifax, not able to go to sea, costing the people of this country $450,000 a year; and the Rainbow, another ship twenty-five years old, also absolutely obsolete, tied up to the dock at Esquimalt, costing this country $275,000 a year. This Government saw fit to reorganize the naval service and we have done so; we have put it on an efficient basis; we have done away with 782 naval ratings and civilians that we did not need. We have done all without a single increase in expenditure. Where, then, does the "white elephant" come in? The "white elephant" would have come in if we had continued to spend the money, which we are now spending on a small efficient navy, by keeping these old obsolete ships at Halifax and Esquimalt. Therefore, while some hon. members think the naval question may be of political advantage throughout the country, I want to make it very clear this afternoon that we are carrying out the policy that was put on the statute book in 1910. We are not increasing the naval expenditure by one dollar. We have accepted, as a free gift from the Mother Country-and we thank her for it-the splendid new modern ships that she has given us. While our navy is small, and while I think we are spending a sufficient amount of money at the present time on the Naval Service, this Parliament and the people have the satisfaction of knowing that what we have is a credit to the country and efficient in every way, and that instead of our having a "white elephant" on our hands by accepting these ships, the reverse is the case. We would have had a "white elephant" on our hands had we carried on the inefficient, poor service that we had and the obsolete ships that were lying at the docks of Halifax and Esquimalt.
I will refer just for a moment to our Agrarian friends-I prefer the name "Agrarian"; I do not favour calling hon. members opposite the Farmers' party, because we are aware that the large major-

ity of farmers in this country from coast to coast do not share the radical ideas of hon. members of that party who sit in this House. Therefore, any remarks that I have to make this afternoon, I want it very clearly understood, apply to the radical Agrarian group that is in this House and the people, especially in the western provinces, who follow that group. The large majority of farmers of this country want stable government; they want a moderate policy of protection, and hon. members will ascertain that in a more convincing way when the general elections take place.

speechtext:
When will they take
place?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know the hon.
member is not in any hurry for the elections.

maintopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, I am.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will possess his soul in patience,. I will promise him an election probably in the year 1923, and possibly in the fall of 1922.
I am glad to see the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) in his seat. I always read his speeches with a great deal of interest and I entertain a very high regard for him. I have the famous policy of the Agrarian party in my hand, and I read there a severe condemnation of the protective tariff. The leader of the Agrarian party, of course, wants to wipe out the tariff; but for the information of hon. members and of the country, because the farmers of this country are taking a keen interest in public affairs now, and while they know what policy this party to the right of the Speaker stands for, they are anxious to know how the hon. member for Marquette proposes to make up the revenue of $163,000,000 that we now derive from customs duty, after he has wiped away every vestige of protection, I hope, when he speaks on the Budget in this House, he will explain how he proposes to raise that amount of revenue. It is only a business proposition that I am putting up to-him that he should give the House that information. I recognize that, a couple of years ago, he had some ways and means that he has now discarded entirely. We do not hear any more from the hon. member for Marquette about a land tax, neither do we hear anything from him about succession dues. Therefore, when he rises to speak, as he surely will, on this Budget, I know that he will endeavour to tell the

House how he proposes to get the revenue to take care of the expenditure of the country, and particularly the revenue of $163,000,000 at present derived from the customs tariff. When the hon. member for Marquette was speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the Throne, I heard him make a very extraordinary statement. He said that to his mind there was no reason why the manufacturers of Canada in like business should not compete with the manufacturers of the United States. Being a business man like himself, I was interested and somewhat surprised to hear him make that most extraordinary statement. The hon. member knows that if we had in this country a market of 110,000,000 people, if our turnover was as great as the turnover of similar industries in the United States, of course, Canadians would be able to compete successfully with our American neighbours. But the hon. member for Marquette must know that when an industry is in operation, the cost of production depends upon the turnover. Therefore, it is a very unfair statement to make that Canadian manufacturers, with a limited market, with keen competition, in a country with a population of less than 9,000,000 people and an output so much smaller than that of our American friends, should be able to compete with American manufacturers on even terms. The tariff policy for Canada is the one enunciated by the right hon. the Prime Minister. We want to maintain a moderate protective tariff. The United States since the Civil War has maintained, not a moderate protective tariff, but a very high protective tariff. On this side of the House we are not in favour of a high tariff, but we believe that to make Canada great, in agriculture, in mining, in finance, in manufacturing, and all the other vocations of life, we must maintain a moderate protective tariff in this country. That tariff is not intended solely for, and does not serve only, those who are engaged in dustrial life; it serves equally every citizen of Canada, no matter what his vocation in life may be.
I pass from our Agrarian friends to the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). We have heard enunciated on more than one occasion the fiscal policy on which the hon. gentleman was elected leader of his party at the National Liberal Convention in this city in August, 1919, but for the sake of continuity in my remarks I crave the indulgence of the House while I place that fiscal policy on the pages of Hansard. It is as follows:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of Customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance: First: diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; Second: reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of whidh is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all products of wheat; the principal articles of food; farm implements and machinery; farm tractors, milling, flour and saw-milll machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils; nets, net-twines and fishermen's equipments; cement and fertilizers, should be free from Customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing tupparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff
And the Liberal Party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provision of this resolution When returned to power.
I think it is only fair that when the hon. leader of the Opposition rises in his place in this House to speak on the Budget, he should tell us in very clear terms that he absolutely stands behind this platform on which he was elected. On this side of the House we also expect hon. gentlemen opposite to get up in turn and say that they stand for this fiscal policy that I have just read. Let us for a moment just look at what would happen if such a misfortune . occurred as hon. gentlemen opposite being returned to power. Business is extremely depressed at the present time.

maintopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad, in a
way, to hear my hon. friends say, "hear, hear." There is a special reason for business being depressed at the present time. All business men know that we are now in this year 1921, for the first time in the readjustment period for business since the war. Every manufacturer, every wholesaler, every retailer, throughout this country has large stocks of raw material and finished goods on hand. These goods could he replaced to-day at half their original cost, and consequently business men are not going to make very much profit, if any at all, this year. Then the stocks which had become depleted throughout the world )iave been replenished, and as a consequence Canada, in common with all other nations

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: of the world, feels the depression through which we are passing at the present time. But we have this consolation in this country. Canada is standing this period of depression better than any other country that I know of. The United States is feeling it even more than Canada; the United Kingdom and all the other countries of Europe are feeling it more than we are. In this period of depression my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition and those who sit behind him say: We solemnly pledge that if we are returned to power we will do two things immediately-there will be a general revision of the present tariff, and we will increase the British preference from 33J to 50 per cent. I wonder how my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) is going to square himself with his electors on that policy?
Don't worry.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The constituency
of Quebec East, which my hon. friend represents in this House, is teeming with boot and shoe factories. Now, one of the planks of the platform of the Liberal party which I have just read is that there shall be substantial reductions in the duties on footwear. Therefore, the boot and shoe manufacturers of Quebec East, along with the boot and shoe manufacturers of the rest of Canada, who are already suffering so much from business depression, would not only be placed in a very much worse position if hon. gentlemen opposite should reach the seats of power, but in my judgment, they would be put completely out of business.
Then, how would our great woollen and cotton manufacturers in the province of Quebec and the other provinces of Canada fare with a sweeping reduction of the present tariff and an increase in the British preference from. 33& to 50 per cent? When the leader of the Opposition went down to the city of Montreal, the commercial metropolis of Canada, he never said a word about this fiscal policy of his; I read his speech very, very carefully. He went down to a love-feast there, at which a great banquet was tendered to the ex-Prime Minister of Quebec, Sir Lomer Gouin, and all that the leader of the Opposition had to say on the tariff question was this-that he wanted a new representation in the House of Commons. I would have expected my hon. friend, speaking in the great manufacturing and commercial city of Montreal, to have said that the policy of the National Liberal and Conservative party of moderate protection was a false one, and that the policy

which I have read, which was adopted by the Liberal party in convention in this city in 1919, was the policy for this country. I would have expected him to say: When we get into power we will make sweeping reductions in the tariff, and increase the British preference to 50 per cent, and I will show you how that will increase the population of the city of Montreal and benefit the great manufacturing and commercial institutions of this city. But my hon. friend had nothing whatever to say about the tariff, except what I have stated. However, when he got to the sunny slopes of the Pacific he made quite a different speech. Speaking in the city of Victoria, on September 27, 1920, he said:

We believe that the time has come, indeed, that it is alreaidy long passed, when a downward revision of the tariff is necessary. In this revision we believe should be substantial reductions of the duties on the necessities of life. In other words, on these articles which go to make the food, the clothing, the shelter of the Canadian people; that certain specific articles required for the purpose of consumption, and other articles essential to production, should be piaced upon the free (list.

After a general election.

speechtext:
The feeling in

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I had the honour of making a political tour with the Prime Minister through the beautiful Eastern Townships. He was enthusiastically received by huge crowds of people in every town he visited, including the city of Sherbrooke. Not only that, but the French-Canadian mayors of the various towns visited, in accordance with the customary

courtesy of the French people, not only gave him a most enthusiastic welcome but, everywhere he went, presented him with illuminated addresses in both English and French. In the drill hall in the city of Sherbrooke the Prime Minister was welcomed by a crowd of something like 7,000 people-the building was packed to the doors. Leaving that city and coming to my own city of Montreal a banquet was there tendered to the Prime Minister by the citizens generally of that commercial metropolis, and not by the members of any political party. Over 700 people crowded into the banqueting hall on that occasion, there was not even standing room left, and it was most gratifying to the Prime Minister and myself that the large majority of those in attendance were of the French-Canadian race. What does that mean? That means that any unfortunate feeling that may have been created during the stress of war has passed away. In the province of Quebec there are, of course, large numbers of Conservatives. The people of Quebec are a protectionist people, they do not believe in free trade, they do not believe in increasing the British preference to fifty per cent. They are intensely interested in stable government. They have a distinct leaning towards the party in power that stands for the policy of moderate protection; and difficult as the task may be in that province I can say, in all friendliness to my hon. friends opposite, that when the next general election is over there will be no repetition of the results of 1917-that out of 65 seats 62 Liberals were elected and only 3 members on this side of the House.
Let us have an election, then.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend
from Chambly-Vercheres will get an election in due time, and when that election is over there will be very much larger representation of good French Canadians from the province of Quebec on this side of the House than there is at the present time. To use the words of the hon. member for Red Deer my hon. friends opposite from the province of Quebec are something like Admiral Nelson-they always put -the glass to the blind eye. They fraternize one with the other and can see nothing but victory ahead for themselves-they can see nothing but the maintenance of this "Quebec bloc." One of the sheep has jumped over the walls of the pen and is wandering loose at the present time; in
spite of that however they are confident they can maintain the "Quebec bloc." As to that let me quote from the greatest French Canadian paper in the province of Quebec, a journal that is published and printed in my own city, La Presse.
Oh, oh.

Doubtless, as my hon. friends opposite used to take such great pleasure in reading La Presse in the fighting times when it was standing up for the Liberal party, I am sure they would like me to read the whole of the editorial. Now this is what La Presse says:
In view of these facts there can he but one logical conclusion :

Let us preserve an economic regime which has proved itself so splendidly beneficial, and let us continue protection which is the basis of that regime.
"La Presse" which, ever since its foundation, has never ceased to be the convinced and determined champion of the principle of protection, in the presence of such evident confirmation of the justness of its attitude, remains more than ever convinced that it is essential for the future of Canada to maintain this principle of protection as the basis of our tariff policy.
It is not at this time, when, owing to the universal upheaval caused by the war in the economic field, any error may have disastrous consequences for Canada, that one can reasonably think of abandoning a principle which offers such guarantees for the future. Let us not abandon realities for dreams.

Those opinions are the opinions of the majority of the people from the province from which I come-

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I have only to state that I shall certainly register my vote against the milk-and-water amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), and I am sure all my colleagues will have very great pleasure in also voting against it. Let me repeat, the party to your right, Sir, has a clearly defined fiscal policy of moderate protection. And I hope that hon. gentlemen opposite will tell the House that they stand behind their leader and will support the fiscal policy on which he was elected.

attitude upon that question. He understands the economics of the question just as well as I do, and I cannot understand his position when at one time he mourns thp excess of American imports and at another time says that we must have the foreign capital, which can only come into this country in the form of the imports which he mourns.
Well, what is the problem with which the nation is confronted at the present time? Briefly it is this: that after what my hon. friends opposite assert to have been well on to half a century of the so-called National Policy, in a country of unparalleled resources in extent and value, with only three people to the square mile, we are face to face with a national debt of $2,350,000,-000-largely due to the war, let me admit with the utmost frankness; it need not have been so big if the previous Finance Minister had taxed as my hon. friend is doing, but it is largely owing to the war, nevertheless;-we have a national railway system which showed a deficit of $70,000,000 last year; we have what I am afraid is an utterly unprofitable and losing mercantile marine which has swallowed millions upon millions of the money of the people of this country; our cities are crowded with unemployed, and they are most numerous in Montreal, Vancouver and Toronto, where the shipbuilding escapades of the Government were undertaken to cure unemployment; farm products have already declined to a non-paying basis; and our foreign commerce at the moment as well as our internal trade is declining at an alarming rate. That is the condition of the country, and it is a condition that should give all thoughtful citizens pause. But there is no pause to the Government, for their cure is "more National Policy," as I shall show in a minute. Well, on the ground of ordinary common sense, I should say that if a patient has had a certain treatment for forty-three years and at the end of that period shows this lamentable condition according to the statement of hon. gentlemen opposite, the country would be well advised in doing what I am quite sure it is going to do at the first opportunity-try a change of doctor and a change of medicine. I repeat that the prescription of hon. gentlemen opposite for this condition is more National Policy. It is true that ostensibly the Budget presents but few tariff changes. We are told that this is no time for a tariff revision. My right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) laboured this 
point very hard yesterday. I must confess that I could not see very much in the reasons he urged for this action. A simple answer to all he said would be: If it be not an afterthought to state that the tariff is not being revised because of the unstable conditions the world over, why did you have a tariff commission going from the Atlantic to the Pacific last year?-why the waste of money? If there was to be no tariff revision there surely should not have been a tariff commission last year. That is a simple answer, and I am very much afraid that the failure to revise the tariff at this session would get a truer, as it certainly would get a better, defence if my hon. friends based it not on the instability of conditions throughout the world but on the well-recognized instability of the Government and its majority.
But is it true that we have no revision? Mr. Speaker, I think not. The Budget gives a revision of the tariff, and a very serious revision upwards. In the first place, what does the one per cent extra on all imports amount to but a raising of the tariff? It is the same operation; call it what you like, it is an increase of the import duties on goods coming into the country, and on almost all goods. There are exceptions, but it relegates quite a large number of articles to the past, as regards the free list. It is an immense increase of the tariff burdens of the people of this country. In the second place, for all practical purposes, the revision, in accordance with exchange rates, in the method of collecting of duties is also a very substantial revision of the tariff upwards. Therefore, it is not a fact to say that we have no revision of the tariff in this Budget, we have a great increase of the tariff. Whether you call these taxes tariff or sales taxes, what the people of this country are concerned to know is the real nature of these taxes and their effect upon the national disease, as I call it, which I venture to describe to this House in simple terms which no one can contradict. Whatever we may call the taxes upon which my hon. friend relies largely for his revenue, they are all taxes upon consumable commodities used by the people in this country. Let there be no mistake about that; that whether they are what are commonly called tariffs, or an increase of import sales taxes, or sales taxes imposed upon goods manufactured in the country, they are all of them taxes upon consumable commodities.

I think that a fourth-form school boy cannot fail to follow the simple process of reasoning by which the inevitable and undoubted elfect of these taxes can be worked out. What is the effect of taxes upon consumable commodities? Its first and immediate effect is to raise the price of the commodity. But if it raises the price, what must of necessity be its next effect? Supposing the article in question to be a suit of clothes; supposing that before these taxes are imposed, the money that any given consumer has to spend on suits of clothes is $100-that that is what his personal Budget will allow him to spend upon clothes. If clothes could be bought for $33 a suit, clearly he could buy three suits with the $100; but if the price were by any chance raised to $50, and he had only $100 to spend upon suits, just as clearly he could buy only two suits. Therefore, the first effect of a tax upon consumable commodities for people of limited income-and that means the vast majority of the people of this country-is to increase the price; and the second, inevitably, is to limit the consumption. These are the elements of political economy which have been taught by these supposedly "obsolete" teachers for at least a century and a half. What follows inevitably on decreased consumption is decreased production. Increase the price of the consumable commodity and you decrease the consumption; decrease the consumption and you decrease the production; and if you decrease the production, you lessen the work of the workmen of the country, you increase unemployment. That is what my hon. friend confessed, in the middle of the fiscal year, that his taxes of a year ago did; it was what he was told at the time they would do, and to that extent the Government of the day in this country, where our economic problem is so simple, are, on account of their fiscal policy, as responsible for a large measure of unemployment as if they had ordered a lockout of the workmen. That is the nature of all these taxes, and that is the method of their operation.
I want to go a little further in my opposition to them and to say that taxes of this kind, whether they are tariff taxes or sales taxes, break the three main principles of taxation which all political economists of note have given their adherence to as sound principles. Taxes, in the first place, should be collected as much as possible in proportion to the ability of the taxpayer to pay. That is simple common
sense. Any one who thinks for a moment will come inevitably to the conclusion that a workman who has to calculate very carefully with his wife on a Saturday night how his week's wages will provide the absolute necessaries of life for himself, his wife and his children, is not a very fit subject for heavy taxes. But these taxes place just as big a burden upon a navvy as they do upon a millionaire. They put a bigger burden upon the navvy than upon the millionaire along many lines, because the navvy wants more clothes in the hard work that he does than the millionaire. As a rule, the navvy has a bigger family than the millionaire, and he is taxed upon the articles of clothing worn not only by himself but by every member of his family down to the baby in its long clothes and its little woollen boots.
The second principle of taxation is that all taxes should be certain, and not arbitrary. If you have an income and pay an income tax, the tax is certain as to time, amount and place, according to the size of your income. But these indirect taxes are absolutely arbitrary. If you buy, you pay, and if you do not buy, you do not pay. In other words, the open-handed, free spender pays taxation; the stingy man who puts his money in the bank gets off paying taxes as regards indirect taxation to the extent that he is stingy. I do not object to any man saving, but I think we ought to have a method of taxation that takes a fair proportion of his savings for the state. Taxes ought to take out and keep out of the pockets of the taxpayer as little as possible beyond what is necessary to carry on the government of the country. In the case of all direct taxation, that is the result; for every dollar collected by income tax or succession duties goes to the Government except a few cents for expenditure in connection with the collection. But in the case of a tariff, we take two, three, four times as much from the taxpayers as the Government gets, the two hundred or three hundred extra per cent going into the pockets of those who are protected under a tariff. That, briefly, is what I have to say about the defects of the Budget so far as I see them.	*
I have said that a clear issue is raised by the Budget, on the one hand, and the amendment on the other. I notice that my hon friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is a little doubtful about the kind of support the amendment is likely to get on this side of the House. I think he expressed a doubt as to how far my hon. friend from
i

North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) and I could sail in the same boat. Minister of Trade and Commerce see such a difficulty in reconciling what he considers moderate divergencies of opinion? I recall that ten years ago this spring, he delivered a speech in the reciprocity debate, and was immediately followed, in a contrary sense, by the present Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie); but they now seem to sit very comfortably in the same Cabinet so far as their personal relations are concerned, though I am bound to say that external evidences from time to time show that they are both afflicted with a similar apprehension as to the results in an election which now cannot long be postponed. A more recent case of reconciliation than that occurs to me. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister, with what I am sure is a grim sense of humour which he manages' to hide most of the time-for he is a very serious-minded man-when he went west took with him my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), and he took him west for the very specific purpose of making him toe the line on tariff matters-and he did some line toeing, all right. (Mr. McKenzie) that for the moment at any rate we are getting along all right. This is a first-rate amendment, and I think the betting is good that my hon. friend from North Cape Breton and Victoria will support it.	%

It cannot be otherwise coming from an Opposition to this Government, because, as I said in a previous debate this session, the principle of protection is typical Toryism. What is the principle of protection? Stated briefly, it is that the consumers of the country without exception should be taxed for the building up in a specific case of a single industry. That is most specific Toryism, according to the whole history of- the creed. Why, when the name Liberal was first introduced into the politics of the Old Country, what were the political conflicts of the time? It was about the year 1828 when the term was first applied to the party of progress in the Old Country. And what was happening at that time? The Tory party was engaged in its congenial occupation of defending the privileges of the few and resisting the rights of the many. In the year 1828 the Test and Corporation Acts were repealed. These Acts, which had stood for generations upon the statute books of Great Britain, declared that men should not be members of corporations or attend the public universities unless they were members of a given church, and that church the Church of England. But progressive thought said: You have no right to put disabilities upon the great masses of people who do not think with you religiously. And the Test and Corporation Acts were repealed. In the next year the fight was on Catholic Emancipation. It is well to go back to the old history books occasionally just to know what the fight has been for progress in this world. In 1829 Catholic Emancipation

was carried in the Old Country. It is difficult to believe that before that time, less than one hundred years ago, the people of the dominant church and the dominant party had said that no man who was a Catholic should have civil rights in Great Britain.
That is Toryism.

That was
Toryism in 1829.
It was a Tory Government that repealed that Act. Yes, it was. What are you talking about?

It was a
Tory leader that repealed the Corn laws against the votes of his own party. If my hon. friend wants to stand on that ground, he will take political kudos out of the fact that he himself was elected in the year 1911 for refusing free wheat, because afterwards his leader gave free wheat. The people who carry reforms are not the people who come in at the finish when popular opinion can no longer be resisted, but the people from generation to generation who fight for them against the Tories. Before the year 1832 there were boroughs in England with five people electing two members to Parliament, at the dictation of a duke. Liberal and progressive thought said: This is an iniquity; we will have a Reform Bill. And they carried a Reform Bill against the Tories of that day. In 1846, it is true, Sir Robert Peel carried the repeal of the Corn laws, but in doing it he paid a tribute to Cobden, which I put on Hansard two years ago, as magnificent as a magnanimous man can pay to the real reformer in the case. I do not know whether such a magnanimous tribute is lost or not on my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie). In 1867, against the determined resistance of Toryism, or rather of a Tory leader, the workingmen in the boroughs of England were given the vote. Again, my hon. friend would claim that in history it was the Tories that fought for it. Every one knows that the opposite is the truth; but that is the general character of my hon. friend's beliefs. In 1885, the franchise was extended to people of the counties, through the same progressive and liberal influences; and in 1892, incomparably the greatest statesman of the nineteenth century would have saved us from the horrors we meet with in reading our papers morning by morning, in connection with Ireland, by giving a moderate degree of Home Rule to that distracted land. That the policy was right is conceded to-day by those who opposed it at the time. There has been no finer tribute to a dead statesman than was uttered by Lord Curzon, a blue blood of the blue bloods, a Tory of the Tories, when he rose the other day in his place in the House of Lords and said: "I am afraid Your Lordships' House was not wise in regard to previous Home Rule Bills." There is something pathetic about historic Toryism, Mr. Speaker. It is always dying in the last ditch for a forlorn hope, and that is what is being done, I am sorry to say, by one who should be broader at his time of life in regard to this principle of extreme protection in Canada. This is regrettable; it is pathetic to see an antediluvian at 45 years of age. I have said this much in illustration of what Toryism is, and what Protection is; they are interchangeable so far as fiscal matters are concerned. Toryism is always looking after God's chosen few-and they are the few. On the tariff, your typical Tory in Canada says: "Wheat, of course, is the article you produce in abundance, and it would pay the. national debt; but in my riding they grow tomatoes." And even my hon. friend the Minister of Finance gave an illustration of Toryism. He said that butter was the thing. But we shall not pay our national debt by exports of butter and tomatoes; we cannot pay the national debt with surplus tomatoes and surplus butter. Yet that is the attitude of Toryism; look after the tomatoes, never mind the abundant wealth of wheat and cattle produced on your boundless acres in Western Canada.
There are three great needs, in my judgment, for this country at the present time,-and I am avoiding, I think every one will admit who listens to me, the party talk that has somewhat prominently characterized the speeches which I have heard in this debate since the first two were delivered. The first great and urgent need of this country at the present moment is to increase its trade. Now, I know that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has said that a big trade is not always characterized by prosperity, or words to that effect. I do not want to misrepresent him. He said he would not base too strong an argument for the profitableness of trade merely on its bulk. Well, I think my hon. friend is wrong in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, and I am not sure that the hundredth would not be doubtful. May I

give my hon. friend a simple illustration of the point? Why were we prosperous in this country during the war? Not because men were killing one another. We were prosperous because we had a big international trade; that was undoubtedly the source of our prosperity. We were producing tremendous surpluses under the extreme pressure of the needs of the war, and we had a big international trade and were prosperous, beyond the dreams of avarice in some cases. And so it has always been. Does my hon. friend contend that little business is a sign of prosperity, whether it be a firm or a nation in question? As a rule, big business means great prosperity, and we like business to be good. Why, the manufacturers of Eastern Canada at this moment know which 5 p.m. side their bread is buttered on, and they are looking now to the West and wondering how much acreage is going to be placed under cultivation this year. Why? Because they know that a big production, followed by a big sale of western wheat, means prosperity for the whole country. And there is no gainsaying that, as a general principle. So that, as I say, increased trade, and especially increased foreign trade, is the first great need of Canada at the present time.
Now, my hon. friend mentioned the home market in that connection; that was where he got the butter argument. He told us about our eating most of our butter at home. Well, if we had no market abroad, poverty would accompany our efforts, and not prosperity. What is the use of talking to the farmers of Canada about the home market? We produce in Western Canada, some years, 300,000,000 bushels of wheat, of which we consume 60,000,000. What would you do with the surplus 240,000,000 bushels if you had no foreign market? How would you dispose of that surplus if you did not take proper steps to get it into the markets of the world? In New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island they grow the finest potatoes in the world, but they use only five per cent of their own product, and even the people of York-Sunbury cannot get up in the night and eat potatoes when they are electioneering. These provinces use only five per cent of their own product, and it is absolutely vital to their interests that ever possible step should be taken to get the markets of New England for their surplus potatoes. That is common sense. Over the rest of Canada, nearly everywhere, the people grow potatoes for their own use, and that is not a TMr. M. Clark.]
particularly difficult trick. Even I, who am a very "mixed farmer" to begin with, made a success of potato growing from the start, and I grow a surplus every year to seed the garden with the next year. But in , these provinces they grow largely in excess of their consumption and their prosperity depends absolutely upon disposing profitably of that surplus. And that is another excellent illustration of the value of the reciprocity pact upon which we voted the other day. I do not want to labour that point further.
Hear, hear.

But in regard to some of my hearers, it might be possible to get a simple figure into their heads, and I should like to tell my hon. friend from North Simcoe that if he is not, I am, alarmed by the fact that in the month of March our foreign trade declined in this country by nearly $100,000,000. Now, it makes a very great difference to this nation at the present moment, in the face of a fact like that, whether our policy is directed to increasing our foreign trade or decreasing it. I have proved, by quotations from the fathers that appeal to the common sense of every man who gives an unbiased attention to what I said, that the effect of the Government's taxes is to decrease consumption, to decrease production, and they will inevitably decrease foreign trade also; and I shall support the amendment because in my humble judgment it points the road to an exactly opposite line of policy.
The second great need of our people at the present time is to reduce the cost of living-we are all agreed about that. I know my hon. friend the Minister of Militia said, in what I think was a weak moment the other night, that a cheap country is not a good country to live in. Well that is all very well-

A good position to leave it at the present moment is just this, where I left my right hon. friend last summer: I left him up against the facts for nine months and his case went out from beneath him. And if I understand him as indicating a wish to contradict my statement-when I say that a lower tariff will make for higher trade and that his policy will decrease trade-then I would advise him to wait for the figures nine months hence. I trust, for the sake of our common country, I am wrong; but if there was any betting in the case I' am afraid that, month by month, my right hon. friend will repent his present attitude. A tariff restricts trade. Why, his nearest 
neighbour in the House (Sir George Foster) who is nearly twice his age and has studied economics all his life-said here once, with the accord of everybody in the chamber, "Of course a tariff-every tariff-must to a certain extent restrict trade." That is what it is put on for. It is to keep the other stuff out so, that the few protected individuals inside the tariff wall can rook the consumer. If a protective tariff did not restrict trade and prevent imports what would be the earthly good of it for building up industries?
Now, I was proceeding, when we had this diversion, to say that the next great need of the moment is to decrease the cost of living. I had got so far as quoting my hon. friend the Minister of Militia as one of the few people who do not believe that, because he said in this House the other evening, that a cheap country is not a good country to live in: Well, I am perfectly persuaded that nine out of ten people in Canada at the present time could do if Canada was just a little cheaper country to live in than it is. If I am not right in that supposition, why have we heard so much about the high cost of living in the past seven years? Why have we carefully scanned the paragraphs in our papers which tell us that it has gone up by a small percentage or down by a small percentage? I will tell my hon. friend the Minister of Militia why those figures have been scanned by the rank and file of the people of this country with earnestness and anxiety: they have been scanned in this way because nine out of ten of the people have felt the cost of living so badly that they have had to calculate very carefully to make ends meet and to get the necessities of life for those who are near and dear to them. It is abject nonsense to say that a dear country is a good country to live in. We have all been wanting to reduce the cost of living. It is absolutely as certain as anything can be-and again my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be my authority-that a tariff increases the price of an article to just about the amount of the tariff. As the amendment proposes to reduce the tariff, in my judgment and in the judgment of every considerable economist who ever lived, you would by reducing the tariff reduce the price of commodities. On this ground also I shall vote for the amendment.
Now I come to the third point. The great need of this country is to build up its industries, and on the principles laid

down so eloquently and so lucidly by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's,
I shall support the amendment, because, little as hon. gentlemen opposite may think so, the amendment's policy will build up the general industry of Canada mpch faster than the policy of the Government.
I see smiles of some doubt when I make a statement of that kind. A great deal of nonsense passes for sense in this world. Binder twine has been free in this country for twenty-three years. That is something the Liberal Government did, anyway. What was the effect upon the industry in Canada? Within that twenty-three years a successful binder twine factory has been established in Welland by an American firm.
An American trust.

My hon. friend can call it just what he likes. I call it a firm. It is a branch of an American firm which has established at Welland under absolute free trade a successful binder twine factory. Let me just pause at this point to intimate that that single fact casts grave doubt upon the only argument that had a semblance of strength in it that I ever heard of for a protective tariff as against the States,-that the tariff is what pulls, so to speak, the factories over-from America to this side. It could not be the tariff in the binder twine case at Welland because there has not been a tariff on binder twine since that factory was founded there. There is another factory making binder twine in which I am more interested as a good Canadian than I am in the Welland factory.
Mr. Speaker-

In Brantford there is a firm called the Brantford Cordage Company. It makes rope, upon which there is a duty, but it also makes binder twine. I take more interest in that firm than in the other on purely national and patriotic grounds. The manager is a born Canadian, and he has established a splendid business there. When the gentleman from whom I get my information visited the factory the other day they were engaged in filling an order for Dublin, in Ireland. This firm, operating without a protective tariff so far as binder twine goes, has sent shipments to the United
States, to the Argentine, to Tunis in North Africa, to South Africa and to Siberia. Now, if that happened in regard to binder twine there, the onus of proving that industries are built up by a tariff is entirely on the shoulders of hon. gentlemen opposite. There are industries and industries in this country.
Mr. Speaker-

Mr. Speaker,
I have been interrupted a good deal and I have very great consideration for whoever is to follow me. However, as my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Hay) has risen I will be very glad to hear what se says.
The question I should like to ask the hon. gentleman is this: Has the establishment of an American binder twine factory in Welland cheapened binder twine to the farmers of Canada?

My hon.
friend's question is really an argument, Mr. Speaker. I am discussing the effect of a tariff upon the building up of industries. My hon. friend understands that. I think that binder twine has been cheapened to the farmer. But that is not what I am dealing with. My hon. friend asks the question for the obvious purpose of making an argument. That sort of question is not permissible in ordinary parliamentary debate. There is nothing in the question. My hon. friend possibly is getting information that he did not have before on the question which I am raising, that the industries of a country generally are not built up by tariffs, but are retarded. What is meant by "industries"? Are railways "industries"? Has the National railway proceeded to enormous success under the protective tariff? It has been under the National Policy. What has that policy done for the railways of this country? What has it done for our shipbuilding?-is not that an "industry"? What has it done for the farming industry? Obviously nothing, because in their great bulk farmers cannot be protected. There is the iniquity and the injustice of the wohle thing as applied to the farming population. Protection is money help; and when you help one industry with money it is a very simple conclusion that the money must come from somewhere, and agriculture bears the entire burden.
What about the Canadian Pacific railway, then?

The Canadian Pacific railway was given the earth to

build itself with. I am going to give my hon. friend, if I may be allowed to pursue my argument, some more facts about Canada. I was talking with a publicist the other day, a journalist of great repute, who knew Almonte very well in 1868. They have some woollen manufactures in Almonte. My friend, who knew it then and knows it now, and is a man with acute powers of observation, tells me that the woollen factories of Almonte were more prosperous in 1868 than they are to-day. I had confirmation of that from a gentleman who called on me recently to speak at Almonte. I asked him; How are your woollen factories? He answered:	Very
depressed. I was talking to a New Bruns-wicker of the highest intelligence and with a splendid memory, who told me that over forty years ago there were in the city of St. John thriving boot and shoe industries; there is not a boot or shoe made there to-day. What has the National Policy done for the boot and shoe industries of St. John? The onus of proof about this industry building all rests upon the shoulders of gentlemen opposite. What is the condition of your manufactures to-day? How many of them are depending on banks at this moment to hold them up? That is not the kind of industry you want to build up. Build them under freedom and they will stand on their own feet and be their own strength the way agriculture is bound to do. I have frequently given the figures as to Britain's manufactures. The broad truth is that Britain neved had any manufactures worth the name until she adopted free trade, her figures in manufacturing exports were infinitesimal; to-day they are the wonder of the world. These are the facts about Canada and the facts about the Old Country. For years hon. gentlemen did not mind my talking in this way, when I was the only man in the country who believed it, but when they know that there will be more believing it than not believing it at the next general election they commence to show a little temper in this business. I am very glad to see it, though what this country wants even more than the things I am dealing with is a change of government.
We have for forty years-

gard to the building of industries and in regard to the building of anything else. There was a Chinaman called Mencius who lived four hundred years before Christ. He was the grandson of Confucius, and he brought a simple figure before his fellow countrymen which only needs to be repeated to impress itself upon the intellect on any hon. gentleman in this House. Mencius said that the industries of a country may be likened to a tree of which agriculture is the stem or bole and the other industries of the country the branches. Now, that old Chink knew more about political econoniy than all the gentlemen opposite put together.

Let me give a single figure more if I may, in support of my contention that our record in the economic field is not equal to the sacrifices of our soldiers. Great Britain raised last year, largely by direct taxation, $7,250,000,000.	Canada raised,
in round figures, $432,000,000. A simple calculation will reveal that, in this country, one-fifth of the population of Britain raised only one-seventeepth of the revenue that was raised in Britain. That going does not make me very proud as a Canadian. The word we all used in the war was: "We are out to fight Germany to the last man and the last dollar." The last man was forthcoming*, voluntarily, in most cases, and he gave not only his last dollar but himself. But we are far from collecting the last dollar or as many dollars as we should do by direct taxation in this country. Let me put that figure in another way. If my hon. friend had gathered, in proportion to population, from the people of Canada as much revenue as was gathered in Great Britain last year, his revenue would be $1,200,000,000. That would make him a little more comfortable about the future than he is at the present moment, in spite of the showing that he has made. My hon. friend could cut a third off that revenue and he would still have a revenue of $800,000,000. He could then meet all the national responsibilities fully and freely and set aside a substantial portion of his income for immediately dealing with the national debt. I have yet to learn that a Canadian is only two-thirds of a Britisher. Why, in every respect in which he has been tested, he is a little over one hundred per cent. Our people in war, in giving, were magnificent. Look at the huge sums that have been left in the hands of the Patriotic Fund and the Red Cross Society for revenue. I speak earnestly on this subject, because, I repeat, we have a great record to live up to, we have a great record of sacrifice and service that we ought to reproduce in our civil life until we have qualified for the moral companionship of those who have died for the country.
I am opposed to this Budget, because its extra burdens, like all its burdens, will

fall, not chiefly upon the rich and the well-to-do, but upon the great masses of the people who have enough to do to make ends meet. The burden of this Budget will fall, first and foremost, upon the returned *men. It will fall especially upon returned men who have taken advantage of the Soldier Settlement Act to settle-upon the land. I told my right hon. friend when he was taking the Soldier Settlement Act through this House that if he settled thousands of returned men upon the land and did not alter his fiscal policy in such a manner as to make it more profitable to farm, what he was doing amounted to a national crime. That is what has come about. There are in Western Canada returned men who, a little over a year ago, gave $1.25 a bushel for seed oats, and in some districts they cannot sell the product to-day at ten cents a bushel.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), in the speech which he delivered this afternoon, talked about boots and shoes, and evidently, he wanted to arouse a little danger to the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) on the part of the boot and shoe industry. What does my hon. friend think of the hide industry? I heard from a farmer, a near relative of mine, the other day, that he sold, in Western Canada, two hides weighing 129 pounds, and he took home the magnificent sum of $1.29; he got a cent a pound for the hides. You cannot get a pair of boots under ten dollars,-I am sorry to say that I am standing in a ten-dollar pair at this moment, and on my farm I would need to skin sixteen full-sized cattle to buy these boots with the hides. I was telling this story to a number of Britishers, and some of them good free traders, in St. Thomas a week ago Sunday, and they said: "It is worse than that here; there was a farmer who brought a hide in the other day, and he could buy only a pair of laces with the proceeds. Yet my hon. friend (Mr. Ballantyne), who is a good stalwart Canadian in many ways and for whom I have a great admiration,-if he had only kept out of politics and especially out of a merchant marine, he was all right-pleads in this House for a duty to help manufacturers of boots and shoes who can get hides for next to nothing and can surely get the leather made out of hides for almost next to nothing, especially when he knows that for the last eight years the boot and shoe industries of Canada have had, not only a huge protection in their home market, but a free entrance

into the United States, because since Mr. Wilson came into power, there has been no duty on boots and shoes in that country.
This burden will fall upon the returned men; it will fall mainly upon the labouring men of the country, the men who always have to calculate earefully to make their income cover their expenditure; it will fall upon the farmers of this country, and it will fall upon the women of the country who sewed and knitted in the war until their eyes were sore with sewing and knitting at one time and with weeping for their lost ones at another. That is why I object to this Budget, because its tariff burdens fall in the main on the rank and file, on the toiling masses, male and female, of this country, and not where they should fall, upon the shoulders of the wealthy who are best able to bear them. Consumption is not the proper thing to tax; consumable commodities are not the proper things to tax. The proper thing to tax is wealth. Wealth is what should be taxed; it is the one place you are sure to get money, and every just and righteous principle demands that sooner or later we shall bring down direct and not indirect taxation.
This is a reactionary Budget. But I have faith in Canada, absolute faith in Canada. She will look after her fiscal matters, and all her other matters. Her record in the war is one which cannot be blotted out. Her history up to date is a glorious one, and her possibilities are practically unlimited. When I stand on my western farm, Mr. Speaker, I sometimes look, as I can look, to the white-topped Rockies, emblems of strength and beauty, and my imagination goes beyond them to the shores of the Pacific, kissed with the warm western winds and lapped with the warm western waves, and I think of the possibilities of almost unlimited commerce with the Orient. Then I look east across the prairies, where we can grow unlimited golden grain, down to Ontario and Quebec with their magnificent material equipment, their history, their traditions-and their feuds, too often unworthy, and would to God that where they are unworthy they should die;- across these I look, and across the Maritime Provinces to the Atlantic where we have a chance of trading with the Old World, and I have unlimited confidence in Canada. There is one obstacle at the present moment in the way of her making a progress which has never been equalled in the world before, and that obstacle she will 2051	'
remove herself when she gets the opportunity, by doing away with the obsolete policies of what I am afraid is a weary, and I am certain is a moribund Administration.

speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT JAMES MANION (Fort William and Rainy River) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a great disadvantage to an ordinary member of Parliament like myself to follow such a speaker as the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Clark). He is always so eloquent and so interesting that it is difficult for an ordinary member to follow him. At the same time one must admit that the hon. gentleman is always consistent, as he showed in his very fine peroration to-day, in arguing for the free trade policy for which he has fought in the Parliament of Canada for very many years. Sometimes in that eloquence and that consistency he stretches a point almost beyond its elasticity to proye his argument. For example, he pointed out a few moments ago that these taxes which are being imposed by the hon. Minister of Finance will particularly hit the returned men. That is news to me. I do not see how they will hit the returned men more than any other class of people in this country, and I presume that the returned men will be as willing to pay their share of taxation as they were to make greater sacrifices when the war was on.
My hon. friend also stretched a point, a little earlier in his speech, when he was criticizing the Minister of Finance for having advised the ladies of Toronto that they should not import the luscious strawberry out of season, paying for it by exporting the juicy grape, and he pointed out as a reason against giving advice against importation that one of the ways by which we can wipe out the $70,000,000 deficit on the national railways is by such things as importing strawberries into the country and exporting grapes out of it. I think, Mr. Speaker, it would take considerable fruit to wipe out that $70,000,000 deficit.
Another statement which the hon. gentleman made was that the unemployment situation in this country was very severe. I admit that; no one can dispute it. There is a business depression throughout the world, but at any rate the unemployment situation in protectionist Canada is not quite so bad as it is in free trade England, where the Prime Minister a short time ago suggested that the unemployed of that country should emigrate to the colonies.

Then my hon. friend also pointed out another interesting thing. I believe he quoted Adam Smith as saying that Holland had ruined herself by taxing the necessaries of life.

May I correct my hon. friend? I am sure he does not wish to misrepresent me. I quoted Adam Smith as saying that in his day the manufacturers of Holland had been ruined. Everybody knows that Holland to-day is not ruined but is a thriving country.

I am sorry I misquoted my hon. friend; I had no intention of doing so. The correction, however, does not affect my argument. The point I was going to make was this, that if the taxing necessaries of life by customs duties-and this is what I understood my hon. friend to mean-leads to the ruin even of the manufacturers of a nation, it should he remembered that the United Kingdom imposes customs duties on necessaries, to a vast extent. I think I would be correct in saying that the customs duties imposed by the United Kingdom are as high per capita as the customs duties in Canada; that is, there is as much per capita collected by that means in the United Kingdom. The strange part of it is that all these customs duties in the United Kingdom are upon the necessaries of life; they are upon products which are not produced in the United Kingdom; upon tea, sugar, tobacco, (which after all is more or less a necessary of life), coffee and cocoa, and gasoline,' I am reminded by an hon. member; tH+ is a point worth remembering in regard to the taxation of the United Kingdom.
Another point that always strikes me in listening to the arguments of hon. gentlemen who advocate a free trade policy is that they nearly always criticise every form of taxation. They seem to be under the impression that no money needs to be raised. They do not suggest any other method whereby the necessary revenue can be raised.
I would like to say that I was rather surprised to find that my hon. friend from Red Deer is going to support the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). It seems rather peculiar to find an out-and-out free trader like' the hon. member for Red Deer, sailing in the same boat, to use his own expression, with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, who is the same kind of moderate protectionist that I am and other hon. gentlemen on this 
side of the House. It made me feel that perhaps amendments like platforms are things to get in on, and not to stand on, as some one said.
