Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at 6 o'clock I was discussing the speech of the hon. gentleman who had preceded me, the member for Red Deer '(Mr. Clark), and was pointing out the difference between his policy and that ot the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). I was struck ,by the peculiar fact that during the hon. gentleman's speech my hon. friends on the other side, that is to say, the regular Liberal Opposition, cheered the member for Red Deer to the echo on many occasions when he was voicing free trade principles which certainly the Liberal party had never upheld or put into practice when in office to any greater extent than had the party on this side of the House. In this connection, the remarks of my hon. friend from Red Deer brought to my mind the fact that when the member for Shelburne and Queen's was speaking the other day he stated that while he was not advocating a protectionist policy, neither was he propounding free trade principles. He was quite emphatic on that point, and he went so far as to say that nobody in this country was upholding a free trade policy. He declared that the Liberal party was not upholding such a policy, nor was the Agrarian party, nor any other body of men. When I heard the hon. and eloquent member for Red Deer addressing the House this afternoon I could not help thinking that the member for Shelburne and Queen's, as he also listened to the hon. gentleman, must have felt that perhaps he had covered too much territory in the statement which he made the other day. It reminded me of an incident which I once witnessed. A man who was somewhat the worse for whisky was standing in a room, and he boasted that he was better than any man in the company present. No one heeded the remark, and he then declared that he was better than any man in the city. Emboldened by the silence with which this boast was received, he went a step further and said that he was better than any man in the country, and

some one walked up to him and knocked him down. As he got up he said: "I know what is the matter with me; I have covered too much territory." As I say, when I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Red Deer, I thought that the member for Shelburne and Queen's must have felt that he, too, had covered too much territory in saying that nobody was upholding a free trade policy in this country.
Last year, when I spoke on the Budget, I gave many facts dealing with the question of free trade and protection, as they apply to Canada, and in doing so I had occasion to make comparisons between protectionist countries, such as Germany and the United States, and a free trade country such as the United Kingdom. In support of my contentions, I submitted facts rather than theories; because, after all, a theory may be as plausible and logical as you wish, but before it can be accepted, it must stand the test of facts. All who have studied history know that there were theories propounded by Aristotle which had been accepted for many centuries but which finally when tested had to be renounced because they were no longer tenable. In this connection, I trust my hon. friend from Red Deer will not demur to my going back so far in history, because he himself went back four centuries beyond Confucius. Many of the theories of Aristotle which had been accepted by the world for centuries were in the end disproven and shown to be fallacious; and yet it is a peculiar fact that those who uphold a theory on mere theoretical grounds, refusing to subject their reasoning to correction in the light of facts, very often, when they find others opposing them are inclined to describe those with whom they cannot agree as heretics. In so many words, they say: if the facts do not square with our theories, well, so much the worse for the facts.
I do admit, Mr. Speaker, that the theory espoused by my hon. friend for Red Deer is an easy one upon which to base an argument; it sounds plausible and logical enough. But even if it were generally accepted to-day in the economic world, the so-called free trade policy, as it has worked out in the United Kingdom, is not necessarily the best policy for our country. Even assuming that it were accepted as a truism that free trade is the best policy for the United Kingdom, that would not prove it to be the best policy to apply to this country. Why do I say that? The United
Kingdom is a country of small area, immensely developed manufacturing plants, highly developed capital, and fully developed natural resources; and certain other attributes which do not exist in Canada. On the other hand, Canada has an immense area, very great, but undeveloped natural resources, little accumulated capital, and little developed manufacturing plants. So that a theory or a policy that might apply with the utmost satisfaction to the United Kingdom might be highly unsatisfactory to Canada. In referring to free trade in connection with the United Kingdom, I purposely used the qualifying expression "so-called," because it has been fairly logically established that the so-called1 free trade of the United Kingdom is not, as a matter of fact, free trade, but an almost unlimited free import. Free trade should embrace two parties; and as a matter of fact, the United Kingdom is the only country of any importance which has put this policy into practice. So that the United Kingdom, while it has given free import to other countries, has really not participated in the mutual advantages that should characterize free trade.
In my speech of last year, which I shall summarize briefly, so that I may not repeat any arguments I then used, I took up the foreign commerce of some of the different important countries of the world, because foreign commerce is one of the things which those who support the free trade policy boast very loudly of as being one of the prominent assets of Great Britain. I pointed out in that speech that between 1890 and 1913, Germany and the United States, two well known protectionist countries, were making much more rapid progress in their foreign commerce than was the United Kingdom. I pointed out further-and I shall repeat the facts again to-night,

that in many of the European markets Germany was selling more than free trade United Kingdom. I showed that Germany had been outselling the United Kingdom in ten important countries before the war. Just here I may say that most of the facts which I submit in this connection have reference to the pre-war period, because it is hardly fair to base argument on conditions as they are to-day, in view of the unsettled state of world affairs. I pointed out that the national debt, per capita, in Great Britain was greater than in the United States or Germany; and in regard to the general welfare of the people of the United Kingdom and other countries, I proved that conditions Wfn

not as good in the United Kingdom as in some other places, so far as those conditions could be judged from such facts as deposits in the savings banks, immigration and unemployment statistics as given by the trade unions of the various countries concerned. Upon these facts, and upon the authority of various writers whom I quoted, I think I showed that the conditions of the ordinary people in the United States were better certainly than in the United Kingdom, and even in Germany they were probably as good as, if not better than, conditions in Great Britain.
Then I touched on railways-a question to which my hon. friend from Red Deer referred this afternoon-and I showed that the United Kingdom had the highest capitalization of any country in the world, and what was very much more important, that the railway rates in the United Kingdom were higher than the rates in Germany, or France, or Austria and a number of other European countries, and about double the rates of the United States or Canada. I touched on pauperism and I gave statistics from the Statesman's Year Book to show that pauperism in the United Kingdom was certainly as great as in Germany, and perhaps greater, and certainly much greater than in the United States. Finally, I touched upon agriculture which my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) covered so completely last night. 1* pointed out at that time that agriculture in the United Kingdom had practically been wiped out under free frade. When I say "practically wiped out" it had been reduced by about fifty per cent under free trade; that while the United Kingdom imported a very great proportion of her food, none of the other countries in Europe imported so much food as the United Kingdom. Take, for example, the growing of wheat. I pointed out that the United Kingdom was greatly surpassed by France, by Germany, by Austria, by Italy, even by Spain-that Spain doubled in 1913-I think that was the year I gave-the wheat production of the United Kingdom. Then I contrasted with that, the development of agriculture in the United States, where it had gone ahead by leaps and bounds, and I pointed out by figures the extent of the development of the natural resources in that country. That is a resume, in brief, of the speech which I made; and I may say that while a number of speakers who followed me took up the theories I expounded and the conclusion to which I came, none of them disputed the facts, so I thought I could come to the

conclusion that my facts were pretty correct. Indeed I am quite positive they were because most of them were taken from official sources.
Now, Sir, I submit that this question of a tariff policy for Canada is still a very vital one to be decided in the best interests of the country. That is the only interest that I have at heart, because I am neither a farmer on the one hand nor a manufacturer on the other. Since then I have looked over the question more thoroughly I have looked over the records of many English writers and while to-day there are many who still uphold free trade as a theory, there is an increasing number of writers in the United Kingdom who are coming to the conclusion that the United Kingdom has been too generous to its trade rivals in opening its markets freely to them, and there are many who have come completely to the conclusion that the United Kingdom should adopt an entire reversal of policy. Let me mention the name of one writer whose works I found very interesting, John Holt Schooling, a well-known writer in the United Kingdom. H<* has written a book, entitled "The British Trade Book." It is a remarkable work, composed for the greater part of statistics, showing the trade of the United Kingdom in its various branches. This writer comes to absolutely the same conclusions which I came to, only he gives many more arguments and reasons in support of them- he covers the ground in a much more elaborate way. I had not seen the book at the time of my investigations last year although it was written some time before. He points out that although the first edition was issued some six years before the one which I read the facts had never been disputed, and he had come to the conclusion, in brief, that free trade was a brain-spun doctrinaire theory, not based upon facts, and that it was not applicable to any country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to allude to a few of the statements of other speakers -not in this debate but in speeches delivered throughout the country-and first I wish to touch just for a moment on the speech of my hon. friend, the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), who, in one of his speeches, made the statement that anybody who mixed up the question of revenue with the question of protection was not only inconsistent but was attempting to mislead the country. Those were the words the hon. member used himself- that a man who did that was inconsistent

and was attempting to mislead the country. Well, Sir, if the hon. gentleman had said the higher the custom tariff the lower the revenue I would say he was perfectly correct; but to imply, as- he implied, that if you have a protective tariff you cannot get any revenue from it, is going very much beyond the fact. I regret that my hon. friend from Marquette is not in the chamber at the present moment; however, that is not my fault. But I should like to point out to him; what he will no doubt admit, that Canada is a protectionist country. I know he has stated that the protectionist policy which has prevailed in Canada ever since 1878 is harmful to this country. He will therefore admit that Canada is under a protective tariff and yet Canada has raised millions of dollars -yes, hundreds of millions of dollars-[DOT] by that tariff. Then he will no doubt also admit that the United States is a protective country. Before the war the United States had the highest protective tariff in the world and by that protective tariff it raised a revenue exceeding that of any other country. So I think these two facts absolutely refute the statement of my hon. friend that a protective tariff cannot give revenue. In making the statement which he did my hon. friend is simply mixing up prohibition-I mean prohibition of customs-with protection; because if you put a tariff of, say, 100 per cent on a certain line of goods none of these goods come in and therefore there will be no revenue; but a moderate tariff will give a certain amount of protection and a certain amount of revenue. He was mixing moderate duties and restraints on trade, just as in the United Kingdom certain people mix up free trade with free imports. It is another case of theory versus fact.
It recalls to my mind an incident which occurred in the House last year during the debate on oleomargarine. The Minister of Agriculture introduced a Bill on the subject and my hon. friend from Bed Deer got up and spoke. He advocated the free trade theory, in the eloquent manner so easy with him, and he pointed out that if Canada had a free trade policy we would have butter at reasonable prices and there would be no need to bother about oleomargarine. That is a synopsis of what he said. Well, out of curiosity I sent out to the reading room and got a copy of the London Times. There I looked up the price of butter in London and found that the price in free trade England, the wholesale price, was higher than the retail price of butter
in protectionist Canada. That is another instance of theory versus fact.
Now I wish to touch upon the subject of immigration. My hon friend from Red Deer referred to that subject last year- and he said (opposing the right hon. leader of the Government) that emigration from the United Kingdom had increased after 1846, because protection had made the people so poor they could not emigrate previously. Then my hon. friend from Red Deer made this statement-That people do emigrate most when they are most prosperous. My hon. friend is usually very logical and very plausible but it is almost too much of a strain upon our imagination to think that people who are living prosperously in their own country will pack up and go out to practically a foreign country and there perhaps cut a home for themselves out of the woods.
My hon. friend in the same speech said that he wanted cheap goods and he cared not whence they came-speaking I believe at that time on the subject of tobacco. That is a very common free trade argument, and I should like to point out to my hon. friend, that there are countries in the world which are very cheap countries to live in-at least so far as buying things is concerned-and yet they are 'sometimes the most poverty ridden countries to be found. For example take the case of China and India. I believe there are no countries in the world where labour is so cheap-and labour is a good criterion of the price of other commodities in those countries-yet in China we have recently seen thirty-five millions of people brought to starvation, and in India from time to time there have been famines which could hardly be overcome.
I might point out also, Mr. Speaker, that the year before the war I had the pleasure of travelling in Southern Italy, and I well remember when visiting Naples I would hire a carriage for the afternoon and after driving around for two or three hours I would ask my cocher how much I owed him, and he would probably say, "Two lire," which would be about forty cents in Canadian currency. I used to feel ashamed to pay him such a small sum even with a tip added. I point that out because Naples at that time was an exceedingly cheap city to live in, and yet was one of the most poverty-stricken centres I have ever seen.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not trespass too long on the valuable time of the House. First of all, let me congratulate my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) upon the magnificent address that he has delivered. I regret that we lost him in 1917, because I am sure that with his eloquence and his youth he would have been quite an addition to the Liberal forces in this Parliament. I hope, however, that the young sinner will repent and that some day he will find his way across the chamber.
I have listened with a great deal of attention to the Budget speech delivered by my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). I think that on the whole it must be conceded that the hon. gentleman was courageous and frank, and that he is entitled to the sympathy not only of this Parliament but of the whole country in view of the appalling situation in which Canada finds herself today. There will he regret expressed all over the land, however, because of the fact that the hon. gentleman failed to implement the promise which his predecessor made on several occasions on the floor of the House, and which he himself reiterated last year when he delivered his first Budget, that there would be a revision of the tariff. When one speaks of the revision of the tariff, one naturally thinks of a revision downwards. I have, Sir, expressed the opinion that there is regret abroad that there is no revision of the tariff, but I believe that when the Budget speech is read from one end of the country to the other, the country may perhaps be satisfied with the one presentment made by the hon. gentleman, because, though there is no revision in the duties downwards, one can certainly see by glancing over the resolutions introduced by my hon. friend the day before yesterday, that there is at least some revision upwards in the tax bill. I am not at all surprised at what has happened. I have never myself believed that there would
be a revision downwards by the hon. Minister of Finance or his associates in the Government.
The Commission of Inquiry which roamed across the continent from ocean to ocean last fall wis-s an object lesson to every Canadian who followed the events of the day. As my hon. friend passed from town to town, from city to city, from province to province he met delegation after delegation, of farmers, fishermen, manufacturers, labourers, miners, indeed of all classes. I followed very closely the evidence placed before the commission, more particularly in the province from which I come. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance listened complacently to the representations made by the high tariff people, but with some nervousness to the many representations that were made to him by those who favoured a reduction in the tariff. Not only did he show some nervousness on those occasions, but he even took issue with those who dared advocate a reduction in the tariff. As my hon. friend was thus pursuing his inquiry, his leader, the present Prime Minister, nailed to the mast the colours of his party and of the Government. He preached high protection from one province to another and so I lost confidence in the revision-to-be, and it is just as well that there has been no revision at all this year, because one may conjecture what a real revision means. Mr. Speaker, there is amongst the men of my faith an accepted maxim that when Rome has spoken the case is closed-Roma locuta est, causa finita esit. The Minister of Finance and the leader of the Government have spoken without equivocation on the question of the tariff, and for the Canadian people the case is now closed. Canada will have high protection; she will have a high tariff, and I am sure that that will suit my genial friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the special class which he represents.
I listened with great attention to the able speech of my young friend the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River. I am not going to join issue with him, because, indeed, he has proven too much. He has proven that John Bull is very miserable under his abominable free trade policy. That is too much for me. It is true that the evidence which my hon friend adduced in support of his theory is what I might call bookish evidence. It is not based on facts, but on theories propounded by doctrinaires who would be only too happy if the whole world was commercially at war.

Yes, my hon. friend has proven too much, and I do not propose to accept his challenge.
I am not going to discuss here the respective merits of free trade and protection. The Parliament of Canada is not an academy. The Parliament of Canada is a forum, and the people of Canada represented by the Government and by His Majesty's loyal Opposition have to face problems as they are, not as they would have them. I have read in the almanac published a century ago by Benjamin Franklin, the quaint old saying that you must take men and events as they are, not as they should be. I claim to be a practical man, and as a practical man I must face conditions, and not a theory. Living as we do under a regime of protection, and standing as I do for a moderate measure of protection, mind you, for a reasonable measure of protection, nevertheless I cannot help saying that I regret that free trade is not the trade policy of this civilized world. I wish that Canada, if it were possible, but it is not, could have free trade as they have it in England. Free trade, I need not say, is a landmark in the history of the United Kingdom; but not only that, the introduction of free trade during the last century was a distinct landmark in the history of modern civilization.
I cannot but smile when I hear such a student as the right hon. member who leads the Government (Mr. Meighen) hint that free trade has made England a poor country. Last year he told us, in so many words, that under free trade, England had become a nation of remittance men. A nation of remittance men! Free trade England, Sir, during the last war, the greatest of all conflicts that have ever perturbed this wide world, showed of what mettle she was made. During that war, free trade England financed herself, first of all, to the extent of thirty-five billion dollars, and then she financed many of the Allied nations to the extent of eight billion dollars; and free trade England, which suffered and bled during those four years, is to-day paying off her debts to the tune of one billion dollars per year. I wish that my country, Canada, could follow the lead given by that nation of remittance men. But, as I said a moment ago, Canada is not England. Canada is Canada, and in spite of the misrepresentations of the Tory press, in spite of some of the speeches which are at times delivered by hon. gentlemen opposite, 'Canada never had a free trade 
policy embalmed in her statute books. And why? Because Canada, relatively speaking, is a new country, with immense territory extending from ocean to ocean, and over that vast space she has but a very sparse population, and the cost of government, civil and otherwise, is very heavy. Therefore, of necessity, the raising of revenue is a constant problem for this country.
How shall you raise your revenue? How shall you pay for the cost of your Government? There are but two ways of meeting the exigencies of revenue: indirect taxation, customs duty and excise, and direct taxation, that is, income tax. I am pleased that the Canadian people have at last learned how the revenue is raised. So long as Canada had only recourse to indirect taxation to meet her national obligations and the cost of government, and so long as she enjoyed relatively prosperous times, she did not fully realize what it was to raise a revenue. But, Sir, in Parliament, during the war, as the expenditure was growing from year to year, and reaching enormous proportions, it became imperative that recourse should be had to other sources of taxation, and I was one of the first, from my place in the House, to advocate the income tax. The income tax exists in the old countries; it has existed in France for many years. It is the most practical form of taxation, because thereby, the people feel that they have to pay, and they therefore look to their governments for the proper application of the moneys which are taken from them. Canada, therefore, has two systems of taxation, and with the customs, the instrument of taxation is, of course, the tariff. I regret that my brilliant friend from Fort William and1 Rainy River (Mr. Manion) extolled to the seventh heaven, such a barbarous system, because, after all, it is a barbarous system. My hon. friend, who is very fond of history, will find in the elements of political economy, that the origin of the word "Tariff" is traced to the name of a little port in Spain, a country which he compared a moment ago to England. He will find that in Spain in the old days, when the buccaneers roved the ocean, watching for the ships laden with the goods of this world, they would leave the little port of Tarifa and then levy sums of money on the legitimate traders from Britain, France, and other countries. Hence the origin of the word tariff; Tarifa was the
9 p.m. home of the tariff, notwithstanding that it may now obtain in Canada, America, Germany, or elsewhere.

May I say that I was
not lauding the tariff? My position was exactly the position of my hon. friend; I was taking necessities into account.

Now, the war is over,
and the glamour of war has vanished; and my hon. friend who, as he said a moment ago, supported in 1911 the infamous Reciprocity Pact, might come across to this . side, for there is no shackle that should keep him where he is at present, unless it he that his hopes are exalted, and that he anticipates finding himself some day seated next to the Minister of Finance as one of the Cabinet ministers.

It would he a pretty
short stay.

Mr. Speaker, we in
Canada are, of necessity, a protection-given people; but there are different ways of applying that policy. It is alleged in the press and in the House, by way of a taunt to us, that the Liberal party and the party opposite are alike, and that there is no real difference between hon. members on your right, Mr. Speaker, and those on your left, the only difference being as between the party angularly opposite the Minister of Finance, and the rest of the House. Well, Sir, parties in this country must be judged by their methods, by their records, by their accomplishments. Let us eliminate the war period, which I admit was an abnormal one, a period that required of this Parliament, and of the country, more sacrifices than ordinarily in the matter of taxation and expenditure.
Let us take two normal periods of recent history. Surely the party to your right, Mr. Speaker, will not disown the period which saw the birth of the National Policy, from 1879 to 1896. For our part we to your left, Mr. Speaker, are proud of the period that extends from 1896 to 1911. We are proud of the gentleman who, because he was the Finance Minister, personified that golden era which he described last year and yesterday in such eloquent language. Consider the series of deficits which mark the administration of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) from 1883 until 1896- deficits which in 1896-1897 amounted to $519,000. We can compare those deficits with the surpluses which mark the Liberal administration. Thus, the year 1896-97, the last fiscal year for which the Minister of Trade and Commerce was responsible, was marked by a deficit of more than half a million dollars, and the year 1911-1912 the last fiscal year for which the hon. member
for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was responsible, was marked by a surplus of over $37,000,000. Mr. Speaker, I say that I can compare with pride the years when I had the honour to he associated with the Laurier-Fielding administration.
To listen to hon. gentlemen opposite one would imagine that prosperity was nonexistent during that period and that we should forget all about it. It is by reading history and by remembering the past that we may guide ourselves for the future. From 1878 until 1896 no less than one million Canadians drifted to the Republic to the south of us. The population of Canada in 1878 was only 4,078,000. In 1896 it had increased, to 5,086,000 in round figures. In 1901, under the Liberal Government, the population of Canada was 5,403,000 and in 1911 it had grown to 7,158,000. The deposits in chartered banks and savings banks in 1878 were a little over $79,000,000. In 1896 they amounted to a little over $245,000,000. In 1911, thanks to that wave of prosperity which had passed over this country, there was in the savings banks and in the chartered banks the enormous sum of $968,183,000. The total exports of Canadian produce in 1878 were $68,000,000 in round figures; in 1896, $110,000,000; and in 1911, $274,316,000 in round figures. The total export of agricultural products in 1878 was $18,000,000; in 1896, $40,000,000; and in 1911, $82,601,000. Of manufactured products there were exported in 1878, $4,127,000; in 1896, $9,365,000; and in 1911, after the Laurier government had been in office for fifteen years the exports of manufactured products amounted to $35,283,000. I say, Mr. Speaker, that with the same basic policy, but administered by different methods and different men, the Liberal party gave Canada prosperity, whilst hon. gentlemen opposite gave Canada adversity.
Last year, and again yesterday, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's explained how he applied in 1896 the principles that were so successful. He held an inquiry from ocean to ocean. He received the farmer, the fisherman, the miner, the manufacturer, the labourer. Did he insist that those who came before his colleagues and himself should be satisfied with either a high tariff, or a low tariff, or no tariff at all? He listened, and having listened, he returned to Ottawa and framed a tariff policy which was given effect to in the session of 1897. The Liberal and Conservative policies are alike, we are told, and it is even asserted that the duties were higher under the Fielding tariff than they

are under the Drayton tariff. Yesterday the member for Shelburne and Queen's explained fully and to the entire satisfaction of any unbiased mind, that there was a revision downward under his tariff reform, 47 articles were added to the free list, and there was a substantial reduction in 147 other articles. In 1907, ten years later-following- the policy which my hon. friend (Mr Fielding) had adopted of revising the tariff every decade-he held another inquiry from ocean to ocean and as a result there was a further revision downward, and 253 articles were put on the free list.
Even my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance will agree with me, I think, that the establishment of the British , preference was a splendid stroke of policy 

a policy which was acclaimed not only by the Canadian people but by the people of the United Kingdom. It was then that Canada became known throughout the whole world. In order to make that policy effective the right hon. the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier and my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), the then Minister of Finance, obtained from the Mother Country renunciation of the Belgian and German treaties. The establishment of the British preference is a landmark in the fiscal history of Canada. First it was 12 per cent, then it was raised to 25 per cent, and finally to 331 per cent.
What were the results of that policy? We are told by some of the die-hards of the Tory party that the aim of the Liberal fiscal policy, if carried out to its full intent, would be the destruction of our industries. I am glad to see my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) in his seat, for he is one of the beneficiaries of the wise Liberal policy of 1897. If he ever became the business man he is-and every one will admit that he is a good business man -it is because of the policy which was carried out under the direction of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's. We were told that the industries of this country would be wiped out, and my hon. friend cited yesterday the classical phrase of the late leader of the Conservative party, Sir Charles Tupper. Well, 'et us see what happened. In 1S90 the capital invested in our manufacturing industries was in round figures $331,635,100; in 1900, three years after the Fielding policy, the capital invested had reached the figure of $446,916,000; and in 1910, the year which preceded the defeat of the Liberal Government, that capital investment amounted to 
$1,247,583,000. Salaries and wages paid in 1890 amounted in round figures to $79 -000,000; in 1900 to $113,000,000; in 1910 to $241,000,000. The value of products in 1890 in round figures represented $368,000,000; in 1900	$418,000,000; in 1910
$1,165,975,000. Those are the results of the sane application of a policy by statesmen who had regard not only to the manufacturers but to the labourers and - the consumers at large.
The British preference, Mr. Speaker, was one of the mainstays' of the Liberal fiscal policy of 1897. That edifice of the hon. then Minister of Finance was crowned by the reciprocity pact which he negotiated with the American Government without going on his knees to Washington but at the invitation of the President himself, while during many years before under the Dingley and McKinley tariffs,-which practically prevented Canada from trading with the United States-our statesmen from both parties had been annual pilgrims to Washington.
I for one deeply regret the present attitude taken by the U.S. Congress. These are sad forebodings-the Fordney Bill, replaced the other day by the Young Bill. That measure speaks a language which will create in many Canadian homes sincere regrets that the country went wrong in 1911. As the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's stated yesterday, with a sob of emotion in his voice, Canada could complain before 1911, but after the attitude of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) and his Government and associates, she cannot complain now because she has officially declined to accept the offer made to her. Sir, it is essential that as between Canada and the great American Republic there should be the most cordial relations. As I stated once before, the two countries speak the same language and are governed by practically the same laws, they practise the same religion and share the same ideals. The peoples of the two countries are liberty lovers and God fearing. Although we have a long boundary line between us, it is entirely unfortified and there is no cloud of misunderstanding. We have given a worthy lead to the nations of the world by settling our differences amicably, and I hope there will never be fired a shot in anger by either of the two countries. Since the war of 1812 forty-three questions between the two countries have been settled by arbitration, and because the Treaty of Ghent has been adhered to by Great Britain on the one hand and the United States on the other

324E
there has never been a ripple to speak of in the relations between both countries.
But, as .the British ambassador stated in Ottawa last fall, speaking before the Canadian Club, great wars between nations are generally if not always preceded by commercial quarrels. Why should we in Canada or they in the United States pick a quarrel in respect to matters affecting our mutual trade relations? I hope, that common sense will prevail. I do not know why our friends of the Tory party are so faint hearted that they will not prosper alongside the United States by exchanging goods with them. I hope that the leader of the Government who is a staunch Britisher, can answer for the loyalty of the Tory party. I know that the leader of the Liberal party and the respected member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), whose devotion to British ideals is well recognized, can answer for the loyalty of the Reformers.
I have, I think, demonstrated, to the satisfaction of this side of the House at all events, that if it is the same basic principle which is followed of necessity-the principle of protection-at least the methods persued are different. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the methods differ. You have only to think of the period between the years 1896 and 1911. Were there any bread lines during those years? Were there any unemployed? I will not say 150,000, because that is the number of unemployed at present in Canada. I will not say 35,000, the number of unemployed in the city of Toronto alone. Were there at any time during those fifteen years 10,000, even 5,000 unemployed persons? There was no unemployment ; the country was busy, almost feverish in its activities. But to-day, what a serious condition of unemployment. Then, there is the decrease in the rural population. I have not the figures for each province but I know that in the banner province of Ontario there has been a marked decrease in the rural population, and there is a loud complaint from rural constituencies that this state of things is demoralizing. The population, is decreasing in rural centres and increasing abnormally in urban centres. Did you find that state of affairs during the Liberal regime? Sir, one must judge of a policy by its results. Do you think, for instance, that during the administration of the Finance Department by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's you would have seen any coquetting with the sugar refiners of Canada one evening and the next morning a quick order given
to the Board of Commerce-the Prime Minister's own creation-to force the Canadian consumer to pay 21 cents a pound for refined sugar at a time when that sugar was being sold at 11, 12 and 13 cents-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do I understand that my hon. friend is referring to me?

Oh, no; my hon. friend is too good a soul, too humane to practice such methods. But he will not deny that all of a sudden last fall the Canadian people realized what protection by the Tory party meant. Here was a case where the Canadian consumers were forced to pay 21 cents, forced to buy from the Canadian refiner only, when across the line that same sugar could be bought at 11, 12 and 13 cents. Mr. Speaker, I thank the Government for having given to the consumers that object leason of what protection is as administered by a Tory Government.
Mr. Speaker, one must judge of a policy by its results. Who will deny that during the fifteen years of Liberal administration the vast prairies of the west became the subject of peaceful invasion on the part of sound and healthy immigrants? I have many quarrels to settle as a member of the Laurier Government, as a Canadian and, shall I say, as a French Canadian, with the ex-Minister of the Interior, Sir Clifford Sifton. But simple truth compels me to say that as Minister of the Interior he had a full grasp of the prob-blem of immigration. I have to admit, Sir, that no Minister of the Interior ever did as much for the Canadian West as Sir Clifford Sifton did. Compare the administration of that regime with that of the present incumbent, and his immediate predecessor, and what is the spectacle that you have? The figures were given by the genial member from Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) as taken from the annual report of the Commissioner General of Immigration of the United States for 1920. For the year 19J8-19 the total number of immigrants coming into Canada from the United States was 44,003 and for the year 1919-20, 48,624. But here is a regrettable statement to make: In 1918-19, 96,075 Canadians left Canada and drifted to the United States. Worse still, in 1919-1920, 143,843 Canadians left Canada for the United States.	The net loss to Canada in
1918-1919 was 52,072 and, in 1919-20, 95,219. I say again that the two policies cannot be the same; because they are so far apart in their results. Under the Lib-

speechtext:
eral regime, the West became a vast expanse of smiling fields, whilst to-day certain sections of the West, if I am correctly informed, are being desolated by this plague of emigration. Surely, Sir, it is not the same policy, and the hon. member for Shelburne and Quleen's (Mr. Fielding) proved that beyond peradventure yesterday as he quoted the famous comment of the late Sir Charles Tupper. For the veterans of the House who remember the kind and genial gentleman who once represented the county of Halton, and was honoured by his political friends with an appointment to the Privy Council, I might quote the late Mr. Henderson, who, speaking in 1902 on the fiscal policy of the Liberal party, used this language:
It was said in the early days of the present tariff that the Liberals had stolen our clothes. What is being said now? I have never said so and I do not consider that thev have done anything of the kind. I am only sorry that they did not, for it would have been better if they had. Their tariff is instead, just the antipodes of ours.
There you have the confession of faith of the leaders of the Conservative party that the two policies are not the same; they are applied differently, and in my judgment, applied with success by the Liberal party. This, however, is |past history. What of the future? The situation is fraught and freighted with heavy responsibilities indeed. It is true that the Canadian people are tendered candid advice on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). Last year, after looking at the rows of figures which constitute our national debt, our deficits, our total- taxation, the right hon. gentleman said:	"Oh, well, we must practise
economy.'' These are his very words:
Stop wasting. Go to work. Produce. Stop grouching and grumbling and we will soon get back to an atmosphere that is bright and happy and hopeful.
Fine words that butter no parsnips. The right hon. gentleman comes back this year, and he is again a spectator of that enormous row of figures, marshalled in his presence, so to speak, like an army, billions of national debt, millions of deficits, millions of taxes, and this time he says: "Oh, it was the war. During war time, the slogan was: more money, more munitions and more clothing." The right hon. gentleman should not forget that three years ago on November next, the armistice was signed. The glamour of war has passed away, and under the fierce light of criticism, this veneer of a pretext disappears completely. During the war my right hon. friend knows 
that money was easy to get, because the people were determined to win the war; they were enthusiastic, and they were ready to make all necessary sacrifices in order to reach the goal of victory. But that glamour has passed away and Canada must now face realities. The right hon. gentleman cannot lure the people any longer with fine rhetoric. During the war rivers of gold, of course, were flowing with such extravagant loans as were launched by my hon. friend's predecessor through the medium of untaxable victory bonds which have created in this country a monied aristocracy. I commend the courage and patriotism of the present Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). The war was over; he launched his loan, and trusted the patriotism of the people. The bonds were not as before, untaxable. Not only have we to face an enormous debt of $2,350,000,000; not only have we to raise this year $435,360,000 on an estimated revenue, according to present legislation, of $372,600,000; but what the people of this country must realize is that besides this enormous Dominion debt, there are provincial debts and municipal debts as well, so that the taxpayer is burdened with a very heavy taxation bill. I had prepared by the Dominion statistician some figures which are very eloquent. The Dominion Government per capita debt in 1920 was $300, in round figures, while the Dominion Government per capita debt, in 1914, was only $43. As regards the provincial per capita debt, I regret the figures do no go beyond 1919, but the figures of this year are certainly greater than those of 1919. Prince Edward Island has a per capita debt of $15.59; Nova Scotia, $29.56; New Brunswick, $64.95; Quebec, $18.90; Ontario, $34.59; Manitoba, $75.30; Saskatchewan, $43; Alberta, $75.83; British Columbia, $52.13. You must add this provincial per capita debt to the Dominion Government per capita debt. Besides that, you have the municipal debts all over Canada. Unfortunately the rural municipalities and the towns do not all send in their statistics to the Dominion statistician, but I have here the figures for a few of the largest cities in Canada, showing the municipal per capita debt:	Montreal, $176.62;
*Toronto, $219.70; Winnipeg, $230.61; Vancouver, $236.21; Calgary, $371.33; Halifax, $109.94; St. John, $85.25; Regina, $291.90; Charlottetown, $59.90.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Are these
gross or net debts?

These are net debts, but gross or net, they make an alarmingly large figure when added together. This country is taxed to the limit, and overtaxed. I appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance on behalf of the taxpayers of this Dominion. I know that my appeal will reach his ears, and I hope his heart too. I could read him letters by the score, from rich men, from people of the middle classes, and from the labouring classes, showing a great deal of anxiety as to how they can face the tax bills of the municipal, provincial and Dominion governments combined. I solemnly ask my hon. friend to live up to his oath of office, as I know he will. Let there be a substantial reduction in the expenditure of the Government, and a policy of retrenchment inaugurated under his regime. In view of this alarming situation, it seems to me that we should concentrate all our efforts on Canada, our country. How should we proceed? I believe in the doctrine which is expressed in the old saying "first things first." How can this Parliament concentrate all its attention and all its efforts on the welfare of Canada?
First, we should revert to responsible Government. This Parliament is not representative of the people of Canada. How can you otherwise account for the lack of interest taken in the proceedings of this House? I have sat in the House of Commons now for 25 years, when Canada never had to face problems such as she is facing now, but, Sir, in no past Parliament have I witnessed such a lack of interest in its proceedings. Yesterday I expressed my surprise to my hon. friend who sits at my right, the able and eloquent member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) , that during the address delivered by the right hon. the Minister of Trade ard Commerce, admittedly one of the great orators of this country, a man of very Wide experience indeed, there should be only a handful of members on his own side to listen to him. Quick as a flash came the answer from my hon. friend, "Because this Parliament is not representative of the people. It is an abnormal Parliament which only fills a gap. The people of Canada are intent on having an election." This Government has no mandate, and why should any party sail under false colours? I can quite understand that under the stress of war a coalition Government might be formed, although the history of all coalitions both in England and in-Canada is a sad one indeed, but why 206J
should a party continue to sail under false colours? Mr. Speaker, this is a British country; we have British ideals of government. There is a Liberal party, an historic party; there is a Conservative party, an historic party. Each represents a tradition. Why should a party absorb the names of all the parties, Conservative, Liberal and National? The name of the party opposite is a misnomer. Let the Tories show their true colours; let the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) who is associated with such a great Liberal statesman, let my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy river and other hon. gentlemen who in a moment of weakness joined the Tory party return to the fold. Let me at this point quote what was said not long ago by Mr. Asquith:
My counsel to you is to keep faithful to your old traditions, to safeguard and vivify your organization and never lose sight of that saving quality which alone makes politics a reputable profession for honourable men, that a party exists not to keep power, not to acquire power, hut it .exists for the promotion of great and worthy ideals.
Just think, in a situation such as this, what would have been the attitude of men like Mr. Gladstone? Do you think they would have allowed themselves to be scared by the bogey of bolshevism-
One would almost think that Mr. Asquith was speaking in 'answer to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen):
-into furling the old flag and marching, with bowed head and reversed arms, horse, foot and artillery, into the camp of the enemy?
Mr. Speaker, let us have a return to the fold on the part of those who in their heart of hearts, in their inner consciousness, feel to-day that they are untrue to their life-long principles.
Second, let us have a free press. Is there anything more degrading than the correspondence which has been published recently showing that one of the heads of the Manufacturers' Association of Canada has been summoning editors to his office and then making terms with them? The vast majority of them, I dare say, were true to their convictions and refused to become time servers to the high tariff: association. But is there anything more degrading in public life than the realization that in this young country, with such a great future ahead of it, those whose mission is to inform the constituencies should be under the whip of a representative of the big interests, and who will go the length of poisoning the wells of public opinion? Sir, this very day, in the city of Montreal, there is a case pending before the courts in which Lord Atholstan is

suing the editor of La Patrie for the recovery of a very large sum of money which is alleged to have been paid to secure the support of that paper during the elections of 1911; and according to the press, the defendants are .summoning as their witnesses the ex-Prime Minister of Canada (Sir Robert Borden), and the ex-Minister of Public Works. I have no doubt that both of these gentlemen will appear before the court at Montreal and will leave that tribunal with clean hands; but if it were proven that a party raised from big interests $50,000 or $60,000 to control one paper and one paper only during one campaign, then I say that one must despair of the future of this young country.
Having secured free Parliament and a free press, let us banish patronage forever from the public life of this country. It was said in 1911, Mr. Speaker, that at last the voice of Toronto would be heard during the elections. Will my hon. friend the Minister of Finance listen for one second to the voice of Toronto? As he lives in Ottawa, ithe civil servants in the capital might shout, perhaps, too loudly, and my hon. friend might be deafened by the uproar; but the voice of Toronto has time to mellow before reaching his ears. Here is what I read from the Civil Service Association of Toronto, -in regard to Bill No. 122, as drafted and introduced by that dear old gentleman, the minister without portfolio (Mr. Spinney), who is astray in a field in which he does not belong. The Civil Service Association of Toronto states: The Bill as drafted will provide for :
First: The substitution of political influence instead of merit in the most important appoint-merits to the public service.
Second : The substitution of political influence instead of merit in promotions.
Third: The repeal of the present preference to returned soldiers in the most important appointments.
Fourth: The nullification of the work of classification and reorganization.
Fifth: The introduction of political partisanship, political influence and inefficiency into the public service of Canada,-
from which it will be seen that all incentive to ambition and efficiency i-n the service is removed and servants of the public are again placed at the mercy of patronage mongers.
I may not be in order in discussing a Bill which is now under consideration, but I am only inferentially re-10 p.m. ferring to it, and I say that if you revive patronage, you work against what I think is and should be the aim of the Minister of Finance, namely, the practice of economy and retrenchment.
I said a moment ago that we should concentrate all our efforts on Canada. In 
the name of common sense, let us not embark upon Imperial ventures. The last war was fought for the purpose of ending all wars, and the madness of armaments has gone for ever, I trust. The sabre-rattling business has been consigned to the junk heap. Let us call a holiday in connection with armaments once and for all. There is no necessity at the present time for Canada to spend the millions which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries intends to devote to the naval service. The hon. gentleman can well do with at least one half of that amount. For the pride of carrying out, as he said this afternoon,-and no one on the other side seemed to evince any nervousness upon /the statement-the Laurier naval policy, I am quite willing to spend about half the amount which my hon. friend has put in the Estimates, although I do not suppose that for this year or next year, or for the next five years to come, it will be necessary to spend any money at all. But it can patrol the waters of the Atlantic and the Pacific, and we can have our naval academies and yards open; but it is unnecessary to spend this large initial amount. The trouble with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine is that he has developed an enormous appetite, he has been diving into millions and millions since the war began, and since he has been in the Government, and he cannot stop. Let me tell him in all sincerity we accept his statement that he has brought his political associates to time, he has made them accept the once abhorred naval policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the principle of autonomy upon which that policy rests, but he should call a halt to more naval expenditure. Mr. Speaker, we should cut the frills of the Militia Department. There is no necessity for the Militia Department spending twenty millions this year. We can certainly do with twenty-five per cent at most of the amount placed in the Estimates under that head. As regards the mounted police I would send them into our western territories. I say to the Government "Practise economy and retrenchment not by word of mouth but by actual .deeds." This Washington Embassy outlay-well, it is better to write it off. Nobody believes in it and it is $100,000 net loss to the country; or perhaps it is $100,000 to pick up a quarrel with the Mother Country under the shelter of the British Embassy at Washington. The mercantile marine is too costly a toy. Fifty millions spent on that mercantile marine!	1	*
Seventy millions.

Seventy millions spent
on that mercantile marine under present circumstances is nothing short of a scandal. The best authority in this country on shipping is, I presume, a gentleman whom my hon. friend (Mr. Ballantyne), well knows, the Chairman of the Canadian Ocean Services, Mr. Bosworth. Speaking at Vancouver not so very long ago that gentleman said:
"I could get all the ships X want, enough to fill your whole harbour (Vancouver)' here for from $50 to $75 a ton " Therefore, considering this tonnage shrinkage, there has not only been experienced an actual loss in operation, but a serious depreciation i-n capital as well. Last year 1 every ship in operation could have been disposed of for what they cost; to-day it is doubtful whether they could be sold for two-thirds of their cost for this condition, four things are responsible:
(1)	An unlooked-for surplus of ships. (There are 16,000,000 more tons of shipping in the world to-day than at the beginning of the war) ;
(2)	A decline in ocean freight rates. (On some commodities it has been as much as 65 per cent) ;
(3)	Smaller cargoes ; and
(4)	An increase in operation costs; supplies and wages having advanced from between 100 and 300 per cent.
I commend these words to my hon. friend . the Minister of Finance. He must substantially reduce the expenditure and retrench if he hopes to restore the credit of Canada. As was said the other day Canada, for many years to come, will be a borrowing nation. But, Sir, the lending nation will always look at the balance sheet of Canada, and when it sees such a rash programme as the one propounded by the Minister of Marine if it loans Canada at all it will he at such rates that we may well call them exorbitant.
The railway problem has to be met and it is indeed an appalling one. I shall not discuss this subject this evening, but I may have something to say upon it at a later date in the session. The only means I know of to meet this emergency is for the Government to inaugurate a vigorous policy of immigration and of land settlement. I am told that there are in the far West twenty-five million acres of unoccupied agricultural lands, within twenty-five miles of existing railways. No later than yesterday I read from Canadian Finance the following:
The settlement of 20,000,000 acres of lands in Western Canada during the next few years will have far-reaching effects. Divided into approximately 100,000 farms it would mean an influx of 100,000 farmers with their families. The average family numbering five-we would,
therefore, have 500,000 persons added to our agricultural population. It is found that the agricultural population of a country needs an equal population in industrial life which means an addition of 500,000 to the population of the cities, towns and villages of Western Canada.
The increases in national wealth which would result from the accomplishment of the aim of the Western Canada Colonization Association may be summarized as follows:
New wealth brought in by settlers
New wealth brought In by settlers.$ 150,000,000
Net worth of new farm production
in perpetuity	 1,875,000,000
New capital attracted from abroad
for industrial undertakings.. ..	75,000,000
Worth of new wealth resulting from profits on handling new farm production	 500,000,000
Total	$2,600,000,000
This vigorous land policy would increase the production of our farmers, and would thereby increase the freight available for our railway system, thus reducing the deficit.
The great asset of Canada is her soil, the great asset of Canada is the natural resources of her vast territory. After all who shalbpay this debt, this enormous debt, of ours? No doubt the revenue raised by means of taxation will pay a part of that national debt but it is through the farmer and the export of the produce of the farm, through the miner and the export of the produce of our mines, that the national debt of Canada will eventually be paid.
On this point may I call the attention of the Government to the little encouragement which is given to the mining industry. The prospecting, the proving, the developing and the operating of the mines are the four great stages of this industry. In the first three departments money is constantly expended, a very large proportion of it yielding not only no profit but no return whatever-the money is lost. Does it not appear reasonable that those who thus risk their money should be entitled to a square deal and be enabled to purchase such diversified machinery as may be required, selecting the market where the best can be purchased and where the expenditure will go the farthest. In other words, Mr. Speaker, I would like the Government in their fiscal policy to consider the case of the miner and the prospector, as I would like the Government to consider the case of the farmer in the way of cheap agricultural implements. It must not be forgotten that producers of minerals have, in the majority of cases, to compete against the world. Hence they should be safeguarded against enhancement in the cost of the necessary preliminary and ex-

perimental operations, and also against an enhanced cost of development.
Now, let me turn my attention to another subject. I have listened with a great deal of attention this afternoon to the remarks of my good friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. He has been very complimentary to his native province. He has repeated what we have read in the press for the past year, that Quebec is. a sane, sober-minded province, that her people are liberty-loving, law-abiding and God-fearing. I accept those compliments, Mr. Speaker. I regret that my hon. friend during the election of 1917, when he delivered a speech at Hamilton, was not so complimentary about the men from Quebec. Pardon me if I am a litle personal-

-becausq he said on that occasion: "I do not take my Liberalism from the Lauriers, the Lemieux, the Bour-assas and the Lavergnes." What did he mean when he said that, especially about Sir Wilfrid Laurier-and, if I may also ask, about myself? Did he mean that Sir Wilfrid Laurier had no interest in the war which brought the hon. gentleman to the Conservative party? Did he mean that I had no interest in the war? Can he explain what he meant? I will accept his explanation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

My hon. friend by that speech made what I would call in law an innuendo against my loyalty, and I resent that because, as my hon. friend said this afternoon, if in the province of Quebec racially we are French-and we are proud of our ancestry-politically we are British. Then- what was the meaning of that speech about Sir Wilfrid Laurier, his old and trusted leader, who said in 1914 that his heart was in the great conflict, and who proved true to the words he then uttered? During his whole life, including the war period, my revered leader, the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was loyal through and through. And I was loyal, too. But I do not boast of my loyalty; my loyalty does not spring from the lips, it is in my heart.
My hon. friend said that we, the Liberal members on this side of the House, were satisfied at the isolation of our province. First of all, I would remind him that our province is not isolated. The Government is isolated, and my hon. friend is isolated in the aforesaid province. He promised that he would do his best to dissolve what he calls the bloc. Well, he can begin to-morrow or next week in the old riding of Yamaska. I and my friends accept the challenge. I know that my hon. friend will be given a cordial and courteous reception if he comes into the county of Yamaska. I will be there on Saturday next, nomination day, with my good friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). I invite the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, his colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and his other colleague the Postmaster General (Mr. Blondin) to be present on the platform. My hon. friend may say, " But I cannot deliver a speech in French." I will speak in English; my hon. friend will do likewise. I invite the whole press of Canada to send representatives. Our language there will not differ from our language here.
My hon. friend made a false step this afternoon. I could see by the attitude of the right hon. Prime Minister that he felt quite uneasy. When asked by the hon. member for Quebec East if the Government had a candidate in Yamaska, my hon. friend at once answered, " Yes, Mr. Mondou is the Government candidate in Yamaska." My hon. friend says so still, I understand. Well, if Mr. Mondou is the Government candidate, it is well that the House should know what he thinks of the Government, and what is his opinion of the Prime Minister whose candidate he

also is, if one accepts the principle of ministerial solidarity. The right hon. gentleman became Prime Minister last summer after a caucus, not after an appeal to the Canadian electorate. Mr. Mondou was just back from Europe at that time, and that great paper, La Presse, which was quoted with such pride this afternoon by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, despatched one of its reporters to get from Mr. Mondou his opinion of the new Prime Minister. Mr. Speaker, I have crossed swords on many occasions with the right hon. leader of the Government. I differ toto coelo from him. His principles and my principles cannot agree; his policy and my policy are as far apart as night from day. But, Mr. Speaker, I would never for the life of me dare express about the Prime Minister of Canada-who, after' all, is the first citizen of the country- the opinion expressed by his candidate in the present election of Yamaska. Now my hon. friend will see what a false step he made. Remember that Mr. Mondou, in the county of Yamaska, says that he is the Mondou candidate, not the Government candidate, and will have no Government supporters around him. This, of course, is the old trick of 19,11. Here is the text of the interview. On July 8, 1920, one of the reporters of La Presse interviewed Mr. A. A. Mondou, ex-Dominion member for the county of Yamaska, and here is that gentleman's appreciation of the Prime Minister:
The selection of the Hon. Mr. Arthur Meigrhen is the worst that could have been made. Do they take the Canadian people for a lot of imbeciles, since they will impose that narrow-minded man as the head of the Government of this country? He is the most bigoted politician who sits at Ottawa, and with all that, as a minister, an undiluted chauvinist. He sees nothing but the West.
.My hon. friends from the prairies will be very much surprised to hear that.
He has not the breath of mind necessary to enable him to become a Prime Minister. He may represent the West, but not the true sentiment of the West. If one takes into account the public sentiment in the various provinces, I do not believe that he could have one of his ministers re-elected With a Prime Minister like Mr. Meighen the province of Quebec can expect nothing-not only nothing reasonable, but nothing fair. It is an open secret that he has been the High Executioner of the Government during the war period. Consult the public records : the thirty five millions-he is the one who got them from Parliament. The gag-he is the inventor of the gag. In Borden-
I quote ipsissima verba.
-the Canadian people lose an indifferent being, but In Meighen they take a hangman and an autocrat. That man represents the quintessence
of ultra-Toryism. Sir Thomas White would have accepted the task of forming a Government, but he exacted in advance the sanction of a general election, and then he would have made peace with the province of Quebec. But the hon. Mr. Meighen snaps his fingers at Quebec and will treat our province during peace time as he treated her during war time. I am convinced that we shall have elections, but come what may, I will be a candidate in Yamaska.
Now, having' read this to the House- and I assume my hon. friend will accept my English version of it-I again ask him if Mr. Mondou is still the candidate of the Government in Yamaska.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am very glad
Mr. Speaker, that my hon. |friend has given me this opportunity to answer this question. The article that he has just read is, of course, quite familiar to me and to all members, especially those from the province of Quebec. My hon. friend takes everything that he has just read as the gospel truth.
But it is from La Presse.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Quite so, but my hon. friend has lived long enough to know that he must not take for gospel everything that he reads even in the daily newspapers of the city of Montreal. Mr. Mondou will make his reply in good time. I am happy to say that he is the Government candidate in Yamaska.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Gaspe invited the answer to his question, and now that the Minister of Marine has spoken I trust that the hon. member will not expect replies to further questions on the subject, as that would be entirely out of order.

The question, Mr. Speaker, was put by the member for Gaspe, and now the member for Maison-neuve will address the House.
In conclusion, let me say to my hon. friend who has charge of the Yamaska election and of the Government candidate in that election that Quebec is as sane to-day as she was yesterday and so she will be to-morrow. Let me remind my hon. friend that Quebec is as adamant to flattery as she has been to insults, and as she is to corruption and bribery. My hon. friend spoke somewhat lightly about the representation in this House from the province of Quebec; he seemed to treat my fellow members with very scant consideration. It is strange, however, that he and his friends have been systematically poaching on the

Liberal preserves of late. We may be bad fellows indeed, but if perchance we would join hands with him and betray our Liberal faith, perhaps we might be regarded as rather good accomplices. In the elections of 1917 Quebec elected 62 Liberal members out of a total representation of 65. It was Edmund Burke, I think, who said, speaking about the American rebels, that you could not draw up a bill of indictment against a whole people. If Quebec was wrong-well, as it is said of the Pope of Rome, when he speaks ex cathedra, she was in my judgment, infallibly right at the last ele'ction. Quebec, Sir, elected 62 Liberal members out of 65, against the Government and the faction which my hon. friend represents. Quebec to-day is just as much opposed to the Government as she was then. My province is entitled to choose her own associates, her own political partners. We live in a free country. If my hon. friend reads the history of the French Canadian race since it has been blessed with responsible government he will realize that my fellowmen have some regard for honour in public life. A man may become "honourable" by law-that is one thing, but to remain honourable is another thing. Hon. gentlemen on this side do not wish to become honourable only by law; they prefer to remain honourable purely and simply.
In the province of Quebec the people read history; they have some education. They remember that at the beginning of the last century Castlereagh was able to bribe a whole party, even a whole Parliament. But they know also that it was the cause of all the miseries, agitations, contentions, which have since desolated Ireland. Quebec will not be reduced to servitude as the Irish were under the corrupt agencies of Castlereagh. Quebec knows that liberties once lost are never recovered; that honour unsullied, fidelity never wavering, loyalty to political ideals, is, after all, the background of selfrespect. To my hon. friend I say in all earnestness: Quebec is not for sale.

Mr. Speaker, I will not pretend to follow my hon. friend nor to criticise his argument to any extent, for the simple reason, that the best part of his argument at least was a resume of the Liberal regime from 1896 to 1911. As I happened to be a supporter of the Liberal Government at that time, it would look very inconsistent on my part, I am sure, to disagree with the hon.

member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux). I quite agree with what he said regarding the progress of the country during that period. He criticised the Government, however for the price of sugar being kept at 21 cents per pound when sugar was selling in the United States at 11 cents per pound. I was never in favour of the appointment of the Board of Commerce, as any hon. member who has sat in the House with me perhaps, knows. But I will say for the board that when sugar was selling at 30 cents per pound in the United States, they kept the price down in Canada to 23J cents per pound by the hundred pounds. I know very well that when sugar was selling at 30 cents per pound in Detroit, it was selling in our town at 23i cents, and that was the case for some time. They promised, I understand, or it was so stated, that when the price of sugar declined, they would give the refiners in this country an opportunity' to make good what they had lost during the time that the board had kept the refiners down to a losing price when the price of raws was 18i to 21 cents, and they were selling to the public refined sugar at 23 i cents.
The hon. member also said that there was a lack of interest in this Parliament, and that the reason for that was, as has been stated so many times during this session, that Parliament had not the confidence of the country. In ordinary representative bodies such as municipal councils, where a municipal council is not criticised by the public, that is generally because it has the confidence of the people and the people are perfectly satisfied. I take it for granted that the same thing is true in proportion as the sphere of representation grows wider. Therefore, I imagine that the reason why there is not more interest in what is going on in Parliament is that the people of Canada are perfectly satisfied that Parliament will carry on the affairs of the country properly. I therefore cannot agree with my hon. friend in his contention in that regard.
My hon. friend cited some figures with regard to immigration and the settlement of land in the West. In a very short space of time by those figures he not only settled the West, but paid off the national debt. This reminds me of the story of the fellow who invented an eye wash which he was trying to sell at fifty cents a bottle. He sat down and calculated that in the United States there were 50,000,000 people and that at fifty cents a bottle he would have an estimated profit of $25,000,000, because the eye wash was costing him nothing but

the cost of the bottle. I am reminded of that story because' the hon. member was going to fill up the West and pay off the national debt in a short time, according to the figures of the theorist who had compiled them.
I must congratulate the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) upon the Budget that he has presented to the House. In the first place he has increased the sales' tax. I know, by certain letters that I received and by other letters, that a good deal of pressure was brought to bear upon the minister to impose what is called a turnover tax which would have gone down all the way to the retailer. He has refused to impose that tax, and he has confined the sales tax to the manufacturer, the wholesaler and the importer. I congratulate him upon that because I think he is wise in so acting. It would1 be a Jtnost expensive matter to collect a turnover tax from the retailer. There are so many retailers in the country who do not keep proper books that it would have been absolutely impossible to collect the tax and to trace it up properly.
I also congratulate the minister upon dropping the business profits tax. I would have preferred to see the business profitstax dropped at least a year ago, because that tax took away from the manufacturer the money that he should have put in reserve for a rainy day, for the very times that are on us now. Last winter, if the business people and manufacturers of the country had been allowed to retain the profits they made during the last three or four years, they could have continued to employ labour to a much greater extent than they were able to employ it, because they would have had a reserve upon which they could have worked. As it was, some of them had even to borrow money to pay the taxes to which they were exposed. Unfortunately, hanks, like other institutions, have a limit to the amount they can lend to allow manufacturers to pile up goods with the prospect of selling them at some time in the future. Therefore that increased, to a large extent, unemployment this winter throughout the manufacturing sections of Canada.
I congratulate the minister also on not increasing the income tax. It was feared by a good many people that if the business profits tax was taken off the income tax would be increased. As a matter of fact, in my judgment, the minister did not lose anything by doing away with the business profits tax this year, because I doubt if there will be a very great profit in the
ordinary manufacturing or commercial business this year. . I think he will get a great deal more revenue from the income tax as it stands now than he would have got from the business profits tax. Therefore, he showed wisdom in doing away with the business profits tax and retaining the income tax. Many people find fault with the income tax on corporations. Not so much fault is found with the income tax on individuals; but on corporations the income tax is exacted before there is any distribution to the people who make up the corporation, that is, the shareholders. Afterwards, the shareholders also pay income tax. They are allowed, of course, the normal tax on dividends; at least, I presume they will be, as they were in the case of the business profits tax.
Our taxes have to be paid; we have to pay our way, no matter who has to pay the taxes, and again I congratulate the Minister of Finance on his wisdom in seeing, to the best of his ability, that we do pay our way. I think we should have done so during the war more than we did. That brings me to the question of the tariff.
I doubt if the whole people of any country would ever agree on the question of the tariff. There are so many different views expressed with regard to it. It is true that the Minister of Finance travelled from ocean to ocean getting the views of various classes of people on the tariff, but I doubt if he was very, much wiser when he got through than when he started as to what would be best in the interests of the country, because every class of people that came before him, and almost every individual, had a different view as to what the tariff should be. It is true that a good many people expected a revision of the tariff. It is also true that a good many items in the present tariff might quite properly have been reduced. It is equally true that a moderate increase could have been made to a good many items without hurting materially the people who bought the goods. The Minister decided, however, that it was not wise owing to world trade conditions to make a general revision of the tariff this year, and I cannot help but think that he was right. If there was any one thing that popularized the late Laurier Government in this country, and gave honour to the Minister of Finance in that Government, the present member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) it was the stability that he lent to the tariff during those fifteen years. The business world
