speechtext: Will the hon. member please repeat the per capita figures which he gave I think there must be some mis- . take; they should be ten times what he stated.

Perhaps they are; 1
only worked it out in my mind. Perhaps it is $16.30 and $18.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is, no doubt, right.

Yes; I put the decimals in the wrong place. Now, I should like to say a word to the Minister of Finance, in regard to the income tax collections.
I am not in favour of the system of income tax collections which * he has put into force, because it is going to cause a great deal of bother and ill feeling, and in my judgment there will be too many unnecessary fines. It would have been much better to have collected the income tax as he did before, sending the tax sheets to those who should pay and giving them notice that they must have their return in by a certain date. If he did that, then I would be in perfect agreement with him if he fined those who did not pay any attention to the notice. No fine is levied, of course, for any error in addition, but if you make an error in any other respect you are subject to a fine, and it will cause a great deal of confusion if the present system is continued. I trust the minister will see his way clear to readjust matters in some way. Besides that, the papers are too technical at present for farmers. My office at home is continually making out reports for farmers. There is nothing in it for us, but we cannot very well object to making these returns for them because they do not really understand how to do it,
and naturally they come to us for help. I say, the papers are too technical for farmers. I am not much of a mathematician, nor an accountant, but I certainly could devise a much simpler form for farmers to make their returns upon, and if my hon. friend the Minister of Finance cannot find anyone else to assist him in this respect,
I will do so without charge.
Now, coming to the revenue. This, roughly speaking, is in the
11p.m. neighbourhood of $400,000,000;
my hon. friend gives it at $372,600,000, but we will say $400,000,000. The Estimates already tabled, amount to over $582,000,000, and some $9,000,000 extra, altogether over $590,000,000, or nearly $600,000,000. Of course, a good portion of this is treated as loans to the railways. I know that it is no sinecure for the Minister of Finance to finance this country at the present time without criticism from anyone. Personally, I am not going to criticise him, but I will ask some of the other ministers to help him out a bit, because I do not see any other way in which he can make the finances balance than by economy, and I am certainly opposed, as he is, to any more borrowing. Last year income and expenditure did not balance. The Minister of Finance had left over from the year before some $101,000,000 and, as he stated frankly, he utilized that so that he wound up with a small surplus. .Nearly all, or at least a great many of the Estimates have passed, and in my judgment a great deal of this money can be saved without doing the country a bit of harm this year. I know that there is a great attack on the Government for expenditures all over the country. It is a mistake for members to want expenditures in their own sections merely because they desire improvements immediately. Our great public works, of course, will have to go on to a certain extent for the purpose of engaging the unemployed. But take the Department of Railways and Canals, and I am sorry the minister (Mr. Reid), is not here; he can easily save that $300,000, or whatever the vote was that was passed the other night for extending the Trent Valley Canal over to Georgian hay. With all deference to the hon. gentleman, I suggest that it is not worth half a dollar to transportation after it is built. Talk about carrying grain on it! Well, you might carry it in your pocket and sail in the boat. That money could be saved this year. The building of the Welland canal is, in my judgment, a different proposition alto-

gether, because there you have a great transportation system. It' is part of what will be one day the greatest transportation system in the world for carrying the grain of the West, both American and Canadian. However, I do not think it will be necessary to spend $5,000,000 because, unless the system is being built under contract, there ought to be a reduction in the cost of the work before next Fall, and there certainly ought to be a material reduction in the price of labour. You cannot tell me that the cost of living is not coming down. The other day our local paper interviewed the grocers of the town with respect to the price of various commodities, and I have here an excerpt from that paper giving the results of inquiry. If hon. gentlemen will kindly listen I will tell them what those prices are and they will see how much the cost of living has been reduced within the last year. I have not the same faith in the figures compiled and issued by the Department of Labour that other people seem to have, because I have seen those figures analysed, item by item, and they give a very false impression in my opinion about the cost of living-that is if one wishes to live reasonably and we must all live according to our means. These are the figures in . question:

That will give an idea of the reduction in the cost of living in the town that I come from, and the prices there, so far as I know, are practically the same as they are in the cities throughout Ontario.
To what figure has butter been reduced in the hon. member's district.
It has been reduced from about sixty cents down to forty or thirty-five cents.

May I tell the hon.
member that butter is selling in Montreal at twenty-six cents this week.

That is all right; it is a reduction. It hurts the fellow that is selling the butter a little, but still the price is coming down. I say that prices are coming down, and that the cost of building the Welland canal should also be lowered, unless the work is under contract at a certain price, because the cost of labour should be reduced.
Now I am going to speak for a moment about the railways. You cannot tell me that the loss on railway operation cannot be cut if the management of our railways take the bit in their teeth, as it were, and cut off the service where traffic does not warrant that service. Let the railway management call a conference of the heads of the various labour departments and tell them frankly that the wages under the Mc-Adoo award, and as adopted by the Chicago Board, ought to be adjusted. By putting up a bold front and doing as every one of us would do in our own private business we could reduce the losses on these railways this year by $25,000,000 at the lowest calculation. We have to do it, and we have to save these moneys in the various departments. Why? Because the Minister of Finance will find that the revenue from Income Tax will not this year amount to anything like the sum'that it did last year. As for the revenue from sales tax I could name firm after firm that are not selling to-day fifty per cent of what they were selling at this time last year. It will not be ' the fault of the Minister of Finance if the revenue falls off; it will be the fault of all of us, and we should back him up in trying to cut down any expenditure that could possibly be avoided during the coming year. The ministers too must recognize that fact.
I want to talk to the Minister of Immigration for a minute, or two. There is nothing that we want more in this country, in my judgment, to build up Canada and help to pay the national debt than immigration. My hon. friend from Mai-sonneuve was talking about that a few minutes ago but only you cannot do it in the sleight of hand manner that he suggested. We want immigration but we want the right kind. At present we are not going about getting it in the right way. In the first place our agents in the Old Country are too glowing in their statements and our advertising is altogether too roseate. You bring a man out to this country who has, we will say, a thousand pounds, that is $5,000, and you make him believe that he can buy up the

north-west territories for that. Well he cannot. If he buys 160 acres of land, and it is anyway decent it will cost him $20 an acre-that will take $3,200. If he buys implements, and then a reasonable span of horses, and a cow, it will cost him another $1,000. There is $4,200 gone. And what kind of a shack will he be able to build with the balance? He could not build a structure very much better than a doghouse. All his money is gone, and there is no way of his getting a dollar back the first year. Therefore every man that comes to this country with a little money should be induced-no matter whether he is going to settle in the West or not-to work for somebody else for a year until he gets on his feet and learns the, conditions. In the first place, the Interior Department should re-survey all the land in the West and select the areas on which a man can successfully conduct farming operations, and not allow some unfortunate immigrant to come jnto Canada and be immediately correlled by some land agent who will sell him a stretch of sandy soil where he cannot produce anything, or locate him in some section of the country where nothing ever grows. I think that in place of these immigrants being brought to the country, dumped down in Montreal, Quebec, Toronto, or whereever it may be, and allowed to wander off like lost sheep, the Immigration Department should have somebody they <?ould absolutely depend on to take charge of these people the very moment they land, supervise their movements until they are on their feet, and see that they are not robbed of any little means they may have. It is a difficult thing for a man coming to a strange country, no matter how capable he may be, to become acclimatized, as it were, the moment he arrives, and to get to know the ways of the people. Unfortunately up in the West, as in Ontario, when the new arrival get to know the ways of the people he has no means left. I would not allow that. If a man is coming to Ontario to settle, I would very strongly advise him to put his money in the bank and work for a year going around to the threshing bees and the silo fillings in order to learn something about the ways of this county before he invests his money. I would strongly advise the Minister of Immigration to let his agents so instruct those men in the Old Country before they come here. We do not want artisans here.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
allow me, during three days last week some
8,000	people landed at Quebec from five ships. I wonder what sort of machine we should have and what the cost would be to take care of those people for a year.

I would not let them come in flocks of that size. That is because your immigration agents induce those people to come here by holding out to them glowing prospects. That is what they tell me, anyway, and I have discussed this matter with people who have come to this country and then cut their eye teeth and got a little wisdom, and every one of them will tell you the same thing. I would only allow people to come here in such numbers that you can take care of them. Where are those unfortunate 8,000 to-night? I bet a good many of them are sorry they ever came. Not that this country is not one of the best in the world

I believe it is the best country-but at the same time there is reason in all things, and we want only such a number of people to come here each year as we can assimilate by putting them on the land or into business. I have no objection to their going into business if they have the money and they are ready to lose it, because they will certainly lose it if they do go into business.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have got all the evil thoughts out of my mind that I had accumulated fop some time, and as I a-', busy on committees I thought I would take this opportunity of telling the Minister of Immigration what I thought his policy should be. I hope that that policy will be so improved that we will get only the sort of immigrants that we want. He knows -there is nobody wiser than he in this country-just what we want, he knows right well just how to handle those who come, and if he has not the means to handle them right, I am sure this House will vote him the means, for ive want to handle our immigration as a man would manage his business. It is no use his sitting there smiling at me. He knows just as well as I do, a good deal better in fact, just how it should be done, and it ought to be done.
Referring to the Budget, I think the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) did remarkably well last year, and if all his colleagues will help him as they should this year, although revenues are bound to fall, he will come out ahead next year. But he must have the assistance of every member of the Cabinet; he cannot do it all alone. The only way that I know of is for him to put the money in a safe

and stand over it with a gun. But I am quite sure the Cabinet will help him in every way, and I hope that the present stagnation of trade will be relieved by next September.
My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) commented this afternoon on what the Minister of Finance had said to the effect that we wanted big business, but that it was not necessarily paying business. He is quite right. My hon. friend from Red Deer took him up and said that business during war time in this country was a big and a paying business. Nobody denies that, for it was a remarkable time. You could buy anything and sell it for more than you gave generally speaking; but the reverse is the case to-day.
My hon. friend from Red Deer also said that Great Britain had doubled her trade in 1920. Well, more strength to her elbow. I have a very loyal feeling for old Great Britain and her business people. Sometimes we meet Englishmen who come out to this country and we wonder how in the world she has been the pioneer in trade, but when we meet others we begin to understand. I am glad that Great Britain doubled her trade in 1920, but she doubled it not on account of her free trade, but because she still has the greatest carrying power of any country in the world. She also did business, not with the United States her great competitor

but with the Eurq-pean countries where her money was at par and with her colonies. We increased our business with Great Britain nearly double what it was the year before. During the war and until after the armistice in 1918 Great Britain's exports had declined to almost nothing, and even if she did double her export trade in 1920 over that of 1919 she would not have done a very large business. But my argument is that it was not owing to her free trade that she did this business, but because she gave credit to European countries that had to have her goods and where the pound sterling was worth 100 cents on the dollar, as it were, and sometimes was even at a premium. There is where she tried to do business, and in that respect she was wise. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) said this afternoon that our unfavourable balance of trade in respect to the United States was largely owing to our borrowings in that country and to the investment of American capital in Canada. As a matter of fact, the figures with respect to the balance of trade as between Canada and the United States as given by the Finance

Minister did not take into account our borrowings or the investments of American people in Canadian industries; they took into account simply the actual trade in goods. My honourable friend makes fun of the Minister of Finance for warning the ladies not to buy unnecessarily in the United States, but I think that his advice is good. I have no ill-feeling against the United States-none whatever. There are certain goods that we have to buy in that country. I personally am interested in one or two businesses which have to buy their raw material in the United States, for the simple reason that they cannot get it anywhere else, and it hurts very much when we have to pay that 15 per cent rate of exchange. I would advise, then, just as strongly as the Minister of Finance does, that we buy nothing that we can possibly avoid buying until our dollar is worth 100 cents in that country.
We have to have a tariff; what is the use of discussing free trade at this time' Even if it were a proper policy I do not see that we could derive any benefit from it. In speaking on the Budget in 1919, I think it was, I gave a list of farm implements required on a farm of 100 acres in Ontario including tools, machinery, harness, and all necessary equipment. I estimated the life of this equipment at ten years; if implements are properly taken care of they will last that long, some of them longer. The duty oxt this equipment spread over a period of ten years would be $28 a year, or less than one cent a bushel on the grain that the farmer would raise on that 100 acres. So that it is not the tariff that keeps the farmer from succeeding. During these last few years it has been chiefly the high cost of labour. Speaking of unemployment, the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) pointed out that there was no unemployment between 1896 and 1911, under the Liberal regime. Thank heaven we did not have very much unemployment at that time, but condi-ditions were different then. Governments are not responsible for these changes in the commercial life of the world; the war was responsible. Europe cannot buy from us, no matter how willing we are to sell, except on long-term credit, and we cannot afford to sell on long-term credit. Therefore there has been a very substantial fall in the prices of our grains, our cattle, horses, wool, sheep, everything we raise on the farm, practically speaking, even to eggs, and as my hon. friend over there said a minute ago, butter. The prices of these

articles have fallen because there is not the export demand for them that there would be if Europe could buy. But that is not in the slightest degree the fault of tire tariff, so far as the sale of goods in Europe is concerned. As to the price of butter, we are again competing with Denmark, Belgium in England itself. New Zealand lately came into the market very strongly gainst us. Why, last winter New Zealand was exporting butter to Toronto, and so was Venezuela. So that the world, as soon as it hears of a higher market, brings the stuff into that market and we have to compete with the world-unfortunately for us, perhaps, in the effect upon the prices of our goods. But these things will, in my judgment, rectify themselves inside of another year. I do not think we should make up our minds that we are ruined.
I do think that those men who are unemployed in the country should be given an opportunity to work. I would not pay one dollar for the upkeep of any sound man who refuses to work. It is all nonsense to say that he cannot work at his trade. Perhaps he is like the fellow who is a good wood-chopper in the summer and a great harvest-hand in the winter, but who does not live up to either when the proper time comes. You need not tell me that these men who are unemployed and who hqve common intelligence cannot go out on the farm and earn fair pay if they are willing to work. On my farms I have frequently taken young fellows from the cities who never had been on a farm before, and inside a month they were as handy as any of the rest uf the men on the farm. So that I speak from experience when I say that it is all nonsense to contend that these men, if they have the opportunity, cannot learn to work on the farm and do it inside a month, thus earning their living in place of being kept by the Government or by somebody else. Of course I am not speaking of disabled men who were at the war; the country owes them all it can possibly do for them. But I do say that the able-bodied man has just as much right to work as any of us have; I would give him the opportunity -to work and if he did not take it I would not keep him any longer. I would like just once more to say that the Minister of Finance was very wise in postponing a general revision of the tariff for this year, on account of the unsettled condition of the trade of the world. He has shown excellent business capacity in the other taxes that he has imposed, and I hope we will get enough revenue to pay our way.
On motion of Mr. Davis the debate was adjourned.

speechtext:
I understand
that this is entirely formal. The request has been granted. Personally I am sorry that I cannot give the assurance the hon. member desires to attend, but I understand that to be the fact.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
On the motion of Hon. Sir Henry Drayton the House adjourned at 11.50 p.m.
Thursday, May 12, 1921.
